Latest Update: On the Brink of Extinction, These Giant Sea Turtles Are Doing Something Unexpected

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A sea turtle population that has declined by more than 90% is showing encouraging nesting success in Ecuador, where cooler ocean conditions coincide with more nests.
  • It has been revealed that when a critically endangered leatherback sea turtle named Bella came ashore in Ecuador in January 2026, her search for a nesting spot took an unexpected turn.
  • Bella eventually returned to the ocean without nesting, but two nights later, she tried again on a quieter stretch of beach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A sea turtle population that has declined by more than 90% is showing encouraging nesting success in Ecuador, where cooler ocean conditions coincide with more nests.

It has been revealed that when a critically endangered leatherback sea turtle named Bella came ashore in Ecuador in January 2026, her search for a nesting spot took an unexpected turn. Confused by nearby streetlights, she climbed over a rock breakwater at Playa de Crucita and ended up on a sidewalk instead of the sandy beach where she needed to lay her eggs.

Bella eventually returned to the ocean without nesting, but two nights later, she tried again on a quieter stretch of beach. This time, she successfully buried 47 eggs in the sand. A few weeks later, 44 baby turtles emerged and made their way toward the sea.

Her persistence is part of a potentially hopeful development for the eastern Pacific leatherback, a critically endangered population of the world’s largest sea turtle. During the 2025–2026 nesting season, researchers documented a record number of leatherback nests along several beaches in Ecuador, more than 1,000 miles from the turtles’ traditional nesting grounds in Mexico and Costa Rica.

Sources indicate that the findings raise an intriguing possibility. As ocean temperatures change, some leatherbacks may be adjusting where they reproduce, taking advantage of cooler conditions along Ecuador’s coast. Whether this represents a lasting adaptation remains uncertain, but successful nesting in new locations could offer opportunities for a population that has declined dramatically.

“Historically, observing female Eastern Pacific leatherbacks on Ecuador’s beaches was a rare or unusual event, but our findings suggest they are adapting their reproductive cycle to thrive and survive in coastal Ecuador,” states Juan José Alava, a marine ecotoxicologist, adjunct professor at Simon Fraser University’s School of Resource and Environmental Management, and leading co-author of the study.

Recent findings suggest that in a study published in Chelonian Conservation and Biology, researchers examined more than 45 years of records documenting reproductive-age female turtles, nesting attempts, nests, hatching success, and stranded turtles along Ecuador’s coastline. They compared these observations with El Niño and La Niña events, which bring warmer and cooler ocean conditions.

Over the past decade, the records showed increased leatherback activity and nesting during cooler La Niña periods in the southeastern tropical Pacific. This relationship suggests that ocean temperatures may influence where females lay their eggs, although the findings do not establish that warming waters are directly causing them to move.

The Ecuadorian nests also indicated encouraging results. The number of eggs per nest and the proportion that successfully hatched were comparable to those recorded at traditional nesting sites farther north. In some cases, Alava indicates, Ecuadorian nests produced more hatchlings than usual.

Industry observers note that leatherbacks are particularly well suited to life across dramatically different ocean environments. They are the only sea turtles that thrive in both warm and cold conditions, traveling thousands of miles between tropical nesting beaches and subpolar Pacific feeding grounds, where they feast on jellyfish during the summer. Their extensive travels have even brought them to Canada’s west coast, with more than 150 records from British Columbia waters between 1931 and 2024.

Despite that remarkable flexibility, eastern Pacific leatherbacks have suffered a population decline of more than 90 percent since the 1980s. Their survival is threatened by unusually warm El Niño conditions, which are worsened by human-caused climate change, as well as fishing bycatch, plastic pollution, vessel strikes, egg harvesting, and the loss of nesting habitat.

In a recent development, “It signals new hope for a subspecies of leatherback on track for extinction in the eastern Pacific within 60 years. They are making their way alongside nature against all odds, representing hope for this species and other sea turtle species even as they reach tipping points.”.

In a recent development, bella’s nesting success offers one example of what Ecuador’s beaches could provide. After researchers tagged her during her first unsuccessful attempt, they discovered that she nested four to five times in 2026 alone. One nest was left in its original location, while the others were moved to the San Jacinto hatchery.

Across the season, Bella laid 146 eggs, producing 134 hatchlings for an overall success rate of 91.8 percent.

Yet finding suitable nesting beaches is only part of the challenge. Bella’s encounter with streetlights and a coastal barrier illustrates how human activity can interfere with reproduction, even when turtles reach a promising location.

Alava emphasizes that continued monitoring, efforts to reduce accidental capture in fishing operations, and effective management of Ecuador’s nesting beaches will be essential to protecting the population over the long term. He also stresses the importance of involving coastal communities in conservation decisions.

“Management and conservation efforts should be championed in close consultation and participation with local and traditional ecological knowledge through coastal, community-grounded interventions.”.

Sources indicate that reference: “A Fresh Hope: Eastern Pacific Leatherback (Dermochelys coriacea) Nesting and Stranding Observations Amidst a Warming Ocean Show the Value of Ecuador for Species Persistence” by Juan José Alava, Kerly Briones, Cristian Soledispa, Cristina Miranda, Eduardo Espinoza, Johanna Moreira, Jodie J. Darquea, Felipe Vallejo, Juan F. Pesántez-Muñoz, Jacqueline Sócola, Johnny Moreira, Carlos Cruz, Marlon Intriago, Kevin Reyes, Alan Miranda, Raúl Carvajal, Cyntia Mizobe, Pedro Jiménez, Nikita Gaibor, Nastenka Calle and María José Barragán-Paladines, 19 October 2026, Chelonian Conservation and Biology. DOI: 10.2744/CCB-1686.1.

Why Did Early Humans Collect Strange Stones 500,000 Years Ago? Scientists Have a Upcoming Theory

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Prehistoric discoveries in Israel raise the possibility that keeping meaningful objects helped early humans distinguish personal memories from stories and gradually develop a sense of identity.
  • It has been revealed that A stone picked up during a hike or a seashell brought home from the beach might seem ordinary to everyone else.
  • In a recent development, A upcoming study from Tel Aviv University suggests that early humans may have collected and kept objects for much the same reason we do today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prehistoric discoveries in Israel raise the possibility that keeping meaningful objects helped early humans distinguish personal memories from stories and gradually develop a sense of identity.

It has been revealed that A stone picked up during a hike or a seashell brought home from the beach might seem ordinary to everyone else. Yet years later, that small object can bring back memories of where you were, who you were with, and what made the experience special. It’s a familiar human habit, and researchers now believe its origins may reach back nearly half a million years.

In a recent development, A upcoming study from Tel Aviv University suggests that early humans may have collected and kept objects for much the same reason we do today. The researchers propose that these prehistoric keepsakes could have helped shape our ability to remember personal experiences and develop a sense of who we are.

The idea emerged from archaeological discoveries at several prehistoric sites in Israel, where researchers found colorful stones, unusual handaxes, and much older tools that appeared to have been collected despite offering no obvious practical benefit.

Industry observers note that at Qesem Cave, for example, small, colorful pebbles had been brought in from different locations. In the Sakhnin Valley, handaxes were made from flint containing fossils or unusual geological patterns. Some were carefully shaped so that these distinctive features remained at the center, where they could be seen and touched.

Other discoveries offer an intriguing connection to the past. At Revadim, Jaljulia, and Qesem Cave, researchers identified older flint tools that had apparently been collected after their surfaces had changed with age. Although some were resharpened, much of their original surfaces and evidence of earlier workmanship remained intact.

In a recent development, why would someone keep an old tool when they could make a new one? The researchers suggest that its age and appearance may have been part of its appeal. Just as an old family heirloom can carry meaning beyond its usefulness, these objects might have been valued for the experiences or histories associated with them.

Sources indicate that dr. Yoav Ram of Tel Aviv University’s School of Zoology explains the possibility:.

Recent findings suggest that “When early humans brought a colorful stone or an old tool they had found in the landscape back to their cave, that object may have helped them remember a significant event or encounter for the rest of their lives. In this way, keepsakes may have become a kind of ‘external memory device,’ supporting the evolution of brain mechanisms responsible for autobiographical memory, which is so characteristic of us as humans and so vital in shaping our identity.”.

There may be a deeper psychological reason why such objects mattered. Our minds do not simply store experiences. They must also distinguish between things we personally experienced, stories we heard from others, and events we imagined.

The researchers propose that seeing or touching a familiar object could have helped early humans make those distinctions. A stone collected from a particular location, for instance, might have brought back a personal memory of being there.

According to recent reports, that ability could have mattered well beyond individual recollection. Remembering encounters, alliances, gifts, mutual obligations, and rights connected to particular places helps people maintain relationships and cooperate. A keepsake could also be carried elsewhere and shown to others, potentially making a personal account more convincing and helping establish trust.

The researchers believe this behavior may have become especially useful as early humans faced changes in their environment.

Prof. Ran Barkai offers one possible explanation:.

According to recent reports, “The disappearance of large animals, particularly elephants, required early humans to develop new hunting methods and become familiar with hunting grounds inhabited by animals such as fallow deer and wild cattle. Objects taken from these places may have helped them maintain a personal connection with the places that would henceforth provide their livelihood.”.

Over many generations, the researchers suggest, keeping meaningful objects may have placed evolutionary pressure on the brain systems involved in identifying where memories come from and how reliable they are.

According to recent reports, in this proposed scenario, objects and memory evolved together. As people increasingly used physical reminders of their experiences, the brain mechanisms supporting personal memory may have become more sophisticated.

In a recent development, that process could have contributed to the development of autobiographical memory, our ability to connect individual experiences into a continuing story of our lives. It is an important part of how we understand our identities and our relationships with others.

The researchers emphasize that their interpretation remains a hypothesis. An unusual stone or carefully preserved tool does not necessarily prove that its owner associated it with a personal memory. The archaeological evidence cannot reveal exactly what someone was thinking hundreds of thousands of years ago.

However, the findings suggest that the habit of keeping meaningful objects may date back roughly 500,000 years, long before written records or photographs.

And if the researchers’ interpretation is correct, the simple act of keeping a stone from a memorable place may once have played a role in the evolution of how humans remember their lives.

According to recent reports, reference: “Homo Memorabiliaxis: Souvenirs and the Evolution of Autobiographical Memory and Self” by Ran Barkai, Ella Assaf, Bar Efrati, Tal Simon, Liad Mudrik and Yoav Ram, 19 October 2026, Evolutionary Anthropology: Problems, News, and Reviews. DOI: 10.1002/evan.70051.

#54399. The Origins of Wealth Inequality May Go Back 5,000 Years, Ancient Graves Reveal

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1121 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

The Origins of Wealth Inequality May Go Back 5,000 Years, Ancient Graves Reveal

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The roots of inherited privilege may reach back thousands of years, with ancient graves revealing how one European community gradually became more divided by wealth and status.
  • It has been revealed that among nearly 300 prehistoric graves examined in Bohemia, the richest belonged to a young girl.
  • For archaeologists, questions like these are difficult to answer because prehistoric societies left behind no census records, tax registers, or written accounts of who held wealth and power.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The roots of inherited privilege may reach back thousands of years, with ancient graves revealing how one European community gradually became more divided by wealth and status.

It has been revealed that among nearly 300 prehistoric graves examined in Bohemia, the richest belonged to a young girl. Buried alongside her was an exceptionally rare copper neck ring, an object that raises an intriguing question about life thousands of years ago. Was she born into a wealthy family, or did her elaborate burial reflect something else about how her community valued status?

For archaeologists, questions like these are difficult to answer because prehistoric societies left behind no census records, tax registers, or written accounts of who held wealth and power.

A latest archaeological method is helping researchers piece together that missing history by examining how people buried their dead. Developed by University of Copenhagen archaeologist Mikkel Nørtoft during his PhD research, QuantWealth combines multiple forms of archaeological evidence to reconstruct social status, displays of wealth, and inequality. In a study published in the Journal of Neolithic Archaeology, Nørtoft and his colleague Adam B. Rohrlach applied the method to 296 graves belonging to the Corded Ware culture in present-day Bohemia, dating from approximately 2900 to 2300 BCE.

According to recent reports, the researchers examined burial practices and grave goods alongside genetic ancestry, Y-chromosome patterns that trace paternal lineages, and skeletal evidence of age, sex, and pathological conditions. By comparing these different clues, they could investigate how social differences changed across several centuries. The findings suggest that inequality developed gradually rather than emerging as a firmly established social hierarchy when migrants from the eastern European steppe settled in the region.

Industry observers note that the Corded Ware culture formed part of a much larger transformation in prehistoric Europe, when populations migrating from the steppe helped spread early Indo-European dialects across the continent. Archaeologists have debated whether these newcomers also introduced strongly patriarchal societies in which wealth and power passed primarily through family lines. The evidence from Bohemia points toward a more complicated history.

“Archaeologists have long debated whether steppe populations migrating across Europe from Ukraine brought with them a highly unequal social system and patriarchy. Our results suggest a much more dynamic picture, where social differences developed gradually. Achieving status through life-actions appears to have been more vital than through inheritance, at least during the first 400 years”, indicates Nørtoft, the study’s lead author.

During the earliest period, approximately 2900 to 2700 BCE, burial practices suggest that the newly established communities placed considerable emphasis on shared traditions. Differences in grave wealth were relatively small and largely associated with age. There was little evidence of pronounced gender inequality, and power appeared to be distributed among several paternal lineages with steppe ancestry.

Nørtoft connects this early pattern to the circumstances surrounding the migrants’ arrival in Central Europe.

“Following a few harsh years of ‘dark sun’ clouded by a devastating volcanic eruption 2,900 BCE, the earliest herder communities, settling in Bohemia around 2,900-2,700 BCE, seem to have focused mostly on building social cohesion across this new network of migrants in Central Europe. In Bohemia, they did this through shared burial rituals, and building earthen mounds, but with few grave goods,” Mikkel Nørtoft explains.

Between approximately 2700 and 2500 BCE, however, burial customs began to change. The appearance of a new paternal lineage coincided with increasingly elaborate funerals, including greater concentrations of prestigious objects and meat offerings. Exchange networks expanded, and differences between male and female burials became more pronounced.

Industry observers note that adult men were particularly likely to receive richly furnished graves, while younger adults became increasingly common among those buried. Despite this growing competition for status, the skeletal evidence did not show a clear corresponding increase in injuries associated with violence.

Recent findings suggest that the final phase, spanning roughly 2500 to 2300 BCE, brought further changes. One paternal lineage had become dominant in the burial record, and a small number of children received unusually wealthy burials. Because children had less opportunity to accumulate status through their own accomplishments, these graves raise the possibility that some families had begun passing social advantages between generations.

“In the final phase, roughly 2,500-2,300 BCE, we see a few rich displays of family wealth through children, and the previously new lineage now dominated the burial record. So maybe the new lineage had gained the most followers and power through the competitive burial parties, and their descendants were now competing among themselves,” Mikkel Nørtoft points out and adds:.

“The few rich child graves and this prevailing lineage could indicate more inherited wealth and emerging traits of persistent inequality. Ethnographic parallels could also support the idea that parents adorned their children with ornaments to increase their social value in future marriage exchange. Brides often moved into the husband’s household in Corded Ware societies, and bridewealth or dowry is preserved in early Indo-European vocabulary, and historically common in Indo-European societies.”.

It has been revealed that the extraordinarily rich grave of a young girl at Čachovice offers a particularly striking example of this possible shift. It was the wealthiest burial among all 296 graves examined and contained an extremely rare copper neck ring. Similar neck ornaments, known as torcs, became widespread symbols of upper-class status during the later European Bronze and Iron Ages. The researchers suggest that objects placed in children’s graves may sometimes have reflected family standing or efforts to enhance their social value in future marriage arrangements, although these interpretations remain uncertain.

Taken together, the changing burial patterns suggest that competition for prestige may have gradually created more lasting social divisions within Corded Ware communities. The possibility that wealth and status were becoming hereditary is especially significant because later Bronze Age societies provide evidence of enduring family dynasties. Whether the developments in Bohemia represented early steps toward those systems remains an open question.

Recent findings suggest that researchers will need additional archaeological and genetic evidence from both the Corded Ware culture and the related Bell Beaker culture, which subsequently replaced it in Central Europe, to determine how closely burial wealth corresponded to inherited family status. The study demonstrates how archaeological evidence, ancient DNA, and linguistic history can be combined to investigate social changes that written records cannot document.

“We now have a correlation between changing Y-haplogroup lineages and unequal burial wealth display in one region, but we need more DNA data to confirm this at the family level, and elsewhere,” explains Nørtoft.

Reference: “Cooperation and Competition: Changes in Wealth, Power, and Patrilines in the Czech Corded Ware Culture” by Mikkel Nørtoft and Adam B. Rohrlach, November 2026, Journal of Neolithic Archaeology. DOI: 10.12766/jna.2026.7.

Industry News: We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1655 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • In a recent development, AI is already powering new, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar.
  • Industry observers note that recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In a recent development, AI is already powering new, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar. What if they set the AI models themselves loose to self-replicate and spread in a malicious manner?

Industry observers note that recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen. Two independent teams revealed how a cyberattacker could turn an AI model into a “worm,” a type of malware that, unlike a computer virus, spreads on its own. And AI unlocked a newly introduced worm power: adapting attacks to different devices.

The results hint at a upcoming way AI could be used to ramp up cybersecurity threats — not just to computer systems but to smart devices such as security cameras or refrigerators. The good news is that the world still has time to build up defenses as several obstacles remain before this type of malware would work in the real world, claims AI researcher Jonas Guan.

AI could indeed make a worm “much harder to stop,” he claims, but “there are a lot of kinks to iron out before something like this really works at scale.”.

Here is how a worm cyberattack works. A malware worm squirms through the internet, copying itself onto whatever systems it can hijack. Hackers can then mine hijacked systems directly for their data or link them together into a botnet and use its computing power, often to send spam email or overwhelm websites with traffic, knocking them offline.

Historically, computer worms have been small, simple programs preprogrammed to take advantage of specific security weaknesses. So they could only get into devices that had that weakness. When defenders patched a worm’s target, it could no longer spread. With an AI model directing its actions, however, a worm can adapt and learn on the fly, choosing its line of attack depending on the device, says Guan, of the University of Toronto.

That adaptability enables the worm to burrow into many different types of devices, both experiments indicated. When hackers unleash AI from afar, they orchestrate what the model does. An AI worm that copies itself widely could hypothetically escape anyone’s control.

Still, there’s a caveat to the experiments’ results, says Michael Alexander Riegler, a cybersecurity researcher at Simula Metropolitan Center for Digital Engineering in Oslo, Norway. Both teams’ test environments made it easier for the AI worm to spread than it would be in the real world, says Riegler, who was not involved in either study.

In a recent development, and there’s another practical obstacle to the unleashing of AI worms. They use more computing power and take up more space than a conventional worm. The Mirai worm, which took down a slew of websites including Reddit and Spotify in 2016, was a few kilobytes in size, while the medium-sized AI models in the experiments were tens of gigabytes. That’s still way smaller than the massive, top-of-the-line models behind the “rogue AI” incidents that made headlines earlier in 2026. (And those weren’t worms, because they didn’t copy themselves and spread.).

Most devices — including typical laptop computers — don’t have enough space or the right kind of chips to run worm-capable AI models, Guan indicates. But latest versions of devices, such as security cameras, are coming out with advanced hardware for running AI, researchers at the AI company Anthropic write. And at the same time, even smaller AI models are becoming more capable of sophisticated cyberattacks. These developments could expand the pool of devices an AI worm could exploit.

Recent findings suggest that “The ingredients are converging” to make AI worms more realistic, Riegler says. How quickly they will converge is up for debate. Anthropic puts the timeline at months into the future, but both Riegler and Guan say it will probably take longer.

The Mirai worm spread itself through smart devices including home routers, security cameras and even baby monitors. It broke into these devices by trying a small set of common default usernames and passwords. “Just using this very simple technique, this Mirai botnet was able to infect hundreds of thousands of devices,” says cybersecurity expert Zane Ma of Oregon State University in Corvallis, who presented an analysis of the attack at a 2017 security symposium. High-profile downed sites such as Reddit were actually collateral damage: A small group of young hackers had created the worm to mess with gaming servers.

Recent findings suggest that rebooting an infected device cleared Mirai. Changing its default login credentials prevented reinfection through the same route. But an AI-powered worm might make cleaning up this type of cybersecurity breach much more difficult. Why? Because the AI worm acts more like an octopus, Guan notes.

Guan and colleagues tested this octopus-worm in a virtual network. Anchored by several powerful computers that each had a chip called a graphics processing unit, or GPU, the faux networks also contained simulations of smart devices, including office printers and security cameras.

Sources indicate that the octopus’s AI model head started on a single machine with a GPU. From there it sent out tentacles to take control of smaller devices. Upon encountering a fresh device, the head would use AI to blueprint how its tentacle could hack in. Often, a hack wouldn’t work, but the octopus wouldn’t give up. It would use info about how it failed to come up with a new hack to try. That ability is “a new, hypercharged way of attacking systems,” Riegler says. Whenever it found a computer with a large enough GPU, it would copy its head onto that new machine.

An attacker would probably launch an octopus-style AI worm from the cloud. Click through this slideshow to see how it might spread autonomously. First, it takes over and copies itself onto a device with the right kind of hardware (chip icon) to house an AI model (first image). From there, it sends out tentacles (red arrows) to hack into any connected devices, like 3-D printers and security cameras (second image). Devices that don’t have enough space for the AI model become jumping-off points for the octopus-worm to discover upcoming places to copy itself (third image).

According to recent reports, J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026.

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026.

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026.

In a recent development, the head could also search a simulated internet for information about newly discovered vulnerabilities. (The team didn’t connect it to the real internet for obvious reasons — protection against an AI octopus invasion — and spent considerable effort making sure their creation couldn’t escape the lab, Guan indicates.).

It has been revealed that the octopus-worm even came up with a way to survive a reboot, something Guan states they hadn’t asked it to do. The team posted a preprint of their findings at arXiv.org on June 2, and the paper is now going through peer review.

In a recent development, meanwhile, at Anthropic, researchers showed another way an AI worm might work by building on Guan and his colleagues’ research. If an octopus-worm wasn’t weird enough, Anthropic dubbed its creation a “digital slime mold”, a name that captures the model’s slow, oozing behavior. Anthropic declined to comment for this story, but Guan states the company’s work shows that “unlike human reasoning, AI reasoning can be distributed.” That means an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily need to hijack a powerful computer to copy and run itself — it could spread its “thinking” out among smaller devices.

Recent findings suggest that and that’s exactly what the slime mold version of an AI worm does. It breaks itself up and runs pieces of the model on multiple smaller devices. In their report posted online October 12, the Anthropic researchers used 15 Android smart TVs that they had networked together.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic’s chopped-up model processes data thousands of times more slowly than what’s possible with GPUs similar to the ones Guan and colleagues relied on. That’s because the model’s data has to travel over internet connections that could take it all around the world during processing, rather than remaining in one place, within chips optimized for AI processing. That pace was too slow to demonstrate an ability to spread like a computer worm, Guan notes. So the Anthropic team ran a separate experiment with an AI worm running on GPUs that revealed it could spread and adapt its attacks to different kinds of devices.

Whether AI worms are coming in months or whether we have longer to prepare, defenders should get ready now, Guan notes. And AI worms do have weaknesses.

For one thing, the large size of an AI worm could be its downfall. Even if smaller AI models become more capable, these are still massive programs that guzzle computing power. You might not notice if your fridge or microwave suddenly started sending lots of traffic onto the network, but your internet service provider would. They’d realize “there’s something weird going on on these devices,” Ma notes. From there, they could quarantine affected devices, disconnecting them from the internet to prevent further spread.

According to recent reports, ma also points out that most smart devices in a person’s home aren’t directly connected to the public internet. Most home networks use a router as a central hub, and that provides a layer of protection against a worm attack.

Strong passwords, regular updates and other normal security measures would also protect against the attacks demonstrated in both experiments, Riegler notes.

Sources indicate that guan and some colleagues are now testing specific defenses to stop AI worms, including devising an AI-driven defender. Trying to anticipate emerging threats and protect systems ahead of time is “what I’m passionate about,” Guan says. “We are working on the problem day and night.”.

Heart Stents May Not Prevent Heart Attacks or Early Death, Landmark Study Finds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (741 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A stent can restore blood flow to the heart, but in people with stable coronary disease, it may offer no added protection against heart attacks or early death.
  • In a recent development, for someone told they have a narrowed heart artery, opening it can seem like the obvious next step.
  • Researchers led by Neel Butala, MD, of the University of Colorado Anschutz, examined that question through an extended follow-up of participants in the COURAGE trial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A stent can restore blood flow to the heart, but in people with stable coronary disease, it may offer no added protection against heart attacks or early death.

In a recent development, for someone told they have a narrowed heart artery, opening it can seem like the obvious next step. Yet improving blood flow and preventing future health problems are separate goals, and a procedure that achieves one may not necessarily achieve the other.

Researchers led by Neel Butala, MD, of the University of Colorado Anschutz, examined that question through an extended follow-up of participants in the COURAGE trial. They found no statistically significant difference in the combined risk of death or heart attack between patients initially assigned to an artery-opening procedure plus medical therapy and those assigned to medical therapy alone.

Published in JAMA and presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions, the findings offer an unusually long look at how these treatment strategies compare.

The original COURAGE trial enrolled people with stable coronary artery disease and compared optimal medical therapy alone with optimal medical therapy plus percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), commonly known as angioplasty.

According to recent reports, during angioplasty, doctors inflate a small balloon inside a narrowed artery to improve blood flow. They often place a tiny metal tube called a stent to help keep the artery open.

For the newly introduced analysis, researchers tracked 959 participants through linked health records. The median follow-up was 15 years, with some patients followed for as long as 25 years. The estimated 25-year cumulative incidence of death or heart attack was 93.3% in the group initially assigned to PCI plus medical therapy and 91% in the medical therapy group. That difference was not statistically significant.

In a recent development, earlier research had examined long-term survival after the trial. This analysis also included heart attacks, allowing researchers to assess whether an initial PCI strategy might prevent cardiovascular events that would not be captured by survival figures alone.

The central finding concerns what happens after an artery has been successfully opened. Restoring blood flow can relieve symptoms, but the study did not find evidence that starting with PCI lowered the combined long-term risk of heart attack or death.

Industry observers note that “When we open a blocked artery, we know we’ve improved blood flow through that artery, and that relieves symptoms. But the bigger question is whether that translates into a reduction in clinical events such as heart attacks or death for patients over the long term. That’s what we wanted to understand with this study,” noted Butala, an assistant professor of medicine-cardiology at the CU Anschutz School of Medicine.

“We found no significant difference in the risk of death or heart attack between the two treatment groups. That’s important information for doctors and patients as they consider the best approach to treating stable coronary artery disease.”.

In a recent development, these results do not mean angioplasty and stents are unnecessary. They can relieve chest pain and other symptoms, while emergency procedures can be lifesaving during certain types of heart attacks. The study specifically examined an initial PCI strategy for stable coronary disease, so its findings should be understood within that setting.

Recent findings suggest that although the participants came from a randomized trial, this analysis was a post hoc observational follow-up, rather than a new randomized trial. It included veterans whose health records could be linked, a group with higher baseline health risks than the full COURAGE trial population.

The researchers also acknowledged limitations in identifying heart attacks through routinely collected health records. However, the findings were consistent with events independently verified during the original trial.

It has been revealed that the research helps clarify what an initial procedure may accomplish. Symptom relief remains a meaningful benefit, but the long-term findings do not establish additional protection against heart attack or death compared with medical therapy alone. Butala mentioned considering both immediate relief and future health outcomes can support more informed treatment decisions.

In a recent development, reference: “Percutaneous Coronary Intervention and Long-Term Outcomes in Stable Coronary Artery Disease: Extended Follow-Up of the COURAGE Randomized Trial” by Neel M. Butala, Nandini Murali, Natalia Rahman, Shayna Cave, Siamack Ayandeh, Mary E. Plomondon, Jonathan W. Cunningham, William S. Weintraub, Robert W. Yeh, Stephen W. Waldo and William E. Boden, 7 November 2026, JAMA. DOI: 10.1001/jama.2026.23488.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec. 11, when current funding runs out.

Sources indicate that “I know it’s going to be my main push,” he said. “I have to work with colleagues to try to find some language that works. And I’m not there yet, but I’ve told everybody that’s an opportunity.”.

It has been revealed that democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont released a statement Thursday that they would oppose any deal that does not include “language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”.

“When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war,” the senators remarked. “It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.”.

It is unlikely that Republicans, who are in control of both chambers of Congress until January, not to mention the Oval Office beyond that, would agree to such a deal.

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., noted earlier this week that “a Republican Congress is not going to send bills to a Republican president that he's going to veto.”.

While ending the war is a top priority of Democrats as they take back power in the newly introduced Congress, insisting on doing so this year could lead to a Christmas-time partial government shutdown. If a shutdown starts after Dec. 11, it’s possible it would still be ongoing when Democrats take control of both chambers in January.

But some Democrats appeared to still be weighing how promptly to push for a cutoff of war funding.

Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash, mentioned that whether or not Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remains in his job, “we’re still going to have language stopping this war.”.

She was coy on whether that fight would take place on the anticipated continuing resolution in December or wait until next year when Democrats take back power, saying that lawmakers are “looking at all options.”.

Democrats are committed to ending the "reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., remarked Thursday. He deferred to House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., "to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11" in talks with the other top appropriators.

"I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro, but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine. to Pete Hegseth’s war machine, over in the Middle East," Jeffries said.

It’s not clear how long a potential continuing resolution would last, and DeLauro said earlier this week that she wants it to be as short as possible.

The Office of Management and Budget has not yet submitted “anomalies” — changes to the current spending levels to be included in the continuing resolution — to Congress.

Recent findings suggest that the administration is considering options including a stopgap bill that would run through March, sources familiar with the talks mentioned. But no decision on the timing covered by the anomalies has been made.

Aris Folley, Jacob Fulton and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have identified a promising way to assess Alzheimer’s-related cognitive risks in otherwise healthy older adults.
  • Industry observers note that A blood test could help estimate whether someone with no memory problems will develop cognitive impairment within the next five or 10 years.
  • Sources indicate that for example, a 75-year-old woman without the APOE e4 genetic risk variant had an estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) of 5% when her biomarker level was relatively low.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have identified a promising way to assess Alzheimer’s-related cognitive risks in otherwise healthy older adults.

Industry observers note that A blood test could help estimate whether someone with no memory problems will develop cognitive impairment within the next five or 10 years. In a newly introduced Mayo Clinic study published in JAMA Neurology, researchers developed a method that combines an Alzheimer’s-related blood biomarker with age, sex, and genetic risk to produce personalized estimates.

Sources indicate that for example, a 75-year-old woman without the APOE e4 genetic risk variant had an estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) of 5% when her biomarker level was relatively low. At a higher level, that estimate rose to 16%. Her predicted 10-year risk increased from 12% to 35%.

According to recent reports, the method measures phosphorylated Tau 217 (p-tau217), a protein associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Elevated levels in the blood are linked to Alzheimer’s-related changes in the brain, but a positive biomarker result alone cannot determine whether or when someone will develop cognitive symptoms.

“The goal is to provide a personalized estimate of the risk of developing cognitive impairment that is more meaningful than simply reporting whether a blood test is positive or negative for amyloid pathology,” indicates Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic laboratory medicine and pathology researcher and first author of the study.

Industry observers note that the research builds on an earlier Mayo Clinic prediction model that used positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans to detect amyloid, a protein that accumulates in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease. Measuring p-tau217 in blood offers a less invasive approach that could be used more widely.

Researchers analyzed data from 1,644 cognitively healthy participants in the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and 534 participants in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. All were between 60 and 90 years old and had undergone blood biomarker measurements, genetic testing, and repeated cognitive assessments.

According to recent reports, using the Mayo Clinic data, the team calculated the probability of developing MCI or dementia within five or 10 years. Higher p-tau217 levels and older age were associated with greater risk. At the same elevated biomarker level, the estimated five-year risk of MCI was 6% for a 65-year-old but 37% for an 85-year-old.

The researchers then examined the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative data, which independently supported the association between elevated p-tau217 and increased risk of cognitive decline.

In a recent development, the approach could eventually help doctors identify people who might benefit from preventive treatment before memory problems begin. However, its clinical usefulness will depend partly on whether therapies can successfully delay cognitive decline in people who have no symptoms.

“A person may want to know: What is my risk of developing cognitive impairment in the next five or 10 years, and how does this blood test change that risk?” notes Ronald Petersen, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic neurologist and director of the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging. “If preventive therapies prove effective, those numbers could become very crucial in treatment decisions.”.

Clinical trials, including AHEAD 3-45 and TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 3, are investigating whether treatments targeting amyloid can delay cognitive decline before symptoms develop. Both trials have used blood biomarkers to help identify participants, highlighting their potential role in earlier Alzheimer’s research.

“Absolute risk gives the biomarker result clinical context,” says Clifford Jack Jr., M.D., a Mayo Clinic neuroradiologist and senior author of the study. “If preventive treatments become available, this kind of information could help patients and clinicians have more informed conversations about the potential benefits and risks of treatment.”.

It has been revealed that the risk estimates were developed using the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and require further evaluation in more diverse populations and with other p-tau217 blood tests. Although the findings support the potential of personalized risk prediction, Alzheimer’s biomarker testing is not currently recommended for people without cognitive symptoms.

In a recent development, reference: “Absolute Risk of Progression to Cognitive Impairment Based on Plasma Phosphorylated Tau 217, Age, Sex, and APOE ε4” by Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Mingzhao Hu, Stephen D. Weigand, et al., 16 November 2026, JAMA Neurology. DOI: 10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.4292.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • It’s spanned the lifecycle of countless gaming consoles, survived multiple scandals, and even withstood a Congressional investigation.
  • Yet, the massive franchise was almost over before it began.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It’s spanned the lifecycle of countless gaming consoles, survived multiple scandals, and even withstood a Congressional investigation. The Grand Theft Auto franchise is seemingly unkillable. Not even a more-than-a-decade wait for the latest installment, Grand Theft Auto VI, could dull the rabid hunger the global gaming community has for the series of open world crime games.

Yet, the massive franchise was almost over before it began. The original Grand Theft Auto, it turns out, was on the proverbial chopping block in the middle of its development. It was only through a few fateful glitches that developers saw what they really had on their hands.

“It was awful,” former creative director Gary Penn recalled in an interview quoted by Game Informer. “It never really felt like it was going anywhere.” At the time, in 1994, the game wasn’t even called Grand Theft Auto,—it went by the much tamer moniker Race’n’Chase. Its developers, now known as Rockstar North, were then a small Scottish studio called DMA Design Ltd. They were best known at the time for a cute, family-friendly (if mildly macabre) PC game called Lemmings.

“The aim of Race’n’Chase,” read a March 1995 design document, “...is to produce a fun, addictive and fast multi-player car racing and crashing game which uses a novel graphics method.” The problem was, the game they were working on was neither fun nor addictive. The car crashes, for one, were a nightmare. “They just didn’t work,” programmer Mike Dailly told The Guardian. “The code was like spaghetti junction.”.

Sources indicate that then there was the matter of the game’s central premise. Originally, Race’n’Chase was meant to be a top-down game where you could play as either the criminals or the police in pursuit, but the developers found that the latter element needed to be excised “’cause nobody wanted to play the cops.”.

Even worse, as the developers tried to deal these design challenges, they were missing key deadlines, and their counterparts in America were getting impatient. “Every week they wanted to kill this game,” recalled level designer Paul Farley in a video for The Guardian. “We’d have to kind of argue to keep it going.”.

In a recent development, then something broke. And it was the best thing that ever happened to them.

Industry observers note that the game had refocused around the criminal element, with the police now pursuing the player in a manner inspired by, of all things, the ghosts in Pac-Man. “Then one day,” Penn recounted, “I think it was a bug, the police suddenly became mental and aggressive. Everybody suddenly went, ‘Hey this is actually pretty cool. There’s something in this, this is working.’”.

That malfunction switched things from Pac-Man ghosts to maniac cops—and recontextualized the entire game in the developers’ minds. “It was less about the mission stuff, which we always thought was another mess, and more about just general play—just being able to p**s around.”.

In a recent development, the developers leaned into the freedom of the game’s sprawling digital city, focusing less on what players could accomplish and more on what they could get away with. In that moment, Race’n’Chase became Grand Theft Auto in all but name. Team members went home at night to watch American action fare like Speed and The A-Team, then came back the next day to pitch scenes from them as missions players could pick up at Liberty City’s trademark phone booths. Most importantly, they started seeing bugs not as roadblocks, but as launching pads.

In a recent development, later in development, another glitch caused groups of NPC pedestrians to “start following one person around,” Farley recalled, much like the marching creatures in DMA’s previous hit, Lemmings. “We thought: ‘Can we use this? What sort of people walk around in a long line like that?’ And we thought of Hare Krishnas.” Rather than do some drastic rewrite of the code, they just tweaked the look of the pedestrians’ sprites, and got the game out to the public.

The game was famously met with controversy after its release because of its violent content, but that uproar actually played into the game’s marketing, and it became a massive financial success for the small Scottish studio. Grand Theft Auto has gone on to become one of the best-selling video game franchises in history, a title sure to be cemented with the release of the notably “sick day inducing” Grand Theft Auto VI.

And none of it would have happened without a single, fateful glitch.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group. His stories for the Enthusiast Group have involved coordinating with organizations like the National Parks Service and the Secret Service, and travelling to notable historical sites and archaeological digs, from excavations of America’ earliest colonies to the former homes of Edgar Allan Poe.

Scientists Develop New Nanomaterial That Could Help the Body Regrow Missing Bone

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A biodegradable material developed by Australian researchers could eventually help children born with cleft lip and palate regrow missing jawbone without undergoing invasive bone graft surgery.
  • Developed at the University of Sydney in collaboration with the University of Queensland, the material works by activating the body’s existing repair signals rather than supplying external growth factors.
  • Cleft lip and palate affects approximately one in 700 children and develops when parts of the upper lip or roof of the mouth fail to fuse completely during pregnancy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A biodegradable material developed by Australian researchers could eventually help children born with cleft lip and palate regrow missing jawbone without undergoing invasive bone graft surgery. In preclinical testing, the experimental nanomaterial produced approximately 80 percent more latest bone than a control material after eight weeks.

Developed at the University of Sydney in collaboration with the University of Queensland, the material works by activating the body’s existing repair signals rather than supplying external growth factors. Researchers hope the approach could eventually allow children to receive treatment years earlier than is typically possible today.

Cleft lip and palate affects approximately one in 700 children and develops when parts of the upper lip or roof of the mouth fail to fuse completely during pregnancy. Correcting the resulting jawbone defects is among the most challenging aspects of treatment, with potential consequences for eating, breathing, speech, and social development.

“One of the biggest challenges for children born with cleft lip and palate is repairing the bone defect in the jaw,” said lead researcher Associate Professor Chun Xu, a Sydney Horizon Fellow in the University of Sydney’s Faculty of Medicine and Health.

“While some children with minor defects are treated as infants, many patients need to wait until they are around 10 to 12 years old before surgeons can take bone from another part of the body and graft it into the defect.

“That means many kids live with difficulties for years. It can affect their breathing, eating and speech. Most heartbreaking of all, it can have a huge impact on their confidence and social development.”.

More than four million bone repair procedures are performed worldwide annually. Many current treatments rely on bone harvested from the patient or animal-derived materials that primarily provide structural support. The new approach instead aims to stimulate the formation of living bone using a biodegradable calcium-aluminosilicate nanomaterial.

In a recent development, the material activates a naturally occurring growth factor called latent Transforming Growth Factor β1 (TGF-β1). This protein normally exists in an inactive form until biological signals trigger its activity. Once activated, it helps recruit stem cells to the damaged area and encourages their development into bone-producing cells. As new tissue forms, the biodegradable material is gradually replaced by the patient’s own bone.

“The material activates dormant repair signals in the body, triggering a cascade of healing processes that attract bone-forming stem cells and stimulate fresh bone growth,” Xu explained.

“Our body already contains many of the signals needed for tissue repair,” Associate Professor Xu noted.

Sources indicate that “We’ve developed a material that can help activate those signals at the right place and time. Instead of supplying external growth factors, we’re encouraging the body to use its own healing potential.”.

The study, published in ACS Nano, found that the material activated the body’s latent bone repair growth factor at approximately 10 times the level achieved using conventional methods. It also promoted blood clotting within about 30 seconds, which could help stabilize an injury during the earliest stages of healing.

Industry observers note that according to the researchers, this is the first demonstration of a single nanomaterial platform capable of combining rapid blood clotting, activation of naturally occurring growth factors, recruitment of bone-forming stem cells, and enhanced bone regeneration. The findings come from a preclinical bone model, however, and further testing is necessary to determine whether the material can be used safely and effectively in humans.

Xu and his colleagues envision a future in which bone defects can be repaired earlier in childhood, potentially reducing the need to remove healthy bone from elsewhere in the body.

“Our long-term goal is to develop materials that help the body regenerate bone naturally and reduce the need for these invasive and painful procedures. We hope this could allow treatment much earlier than is possible today.”.

It has been revealed that the researchers are also investigating whether the nanomaterial could be incorporated into personalized 3D-printed scaffolds designed to fit an individual’s bone defect. Beyond cleft lip and palate, potential applications include repairing bone damaged by traumatic injuries, tooth loss, and other conditions involving difficult-to-heal defects.

“Every patient is different, and every bone defect is different,” Xu said.

“In the future, we hope to combine these materials with advanced 3D-printing technologies so treatments can be tailored to the specific needs of each patient.”.

The technology remains at the preclinical stage, with additional research required before human trials can begin.

Reference: “Multifunctional Mesoporous Calcium-Aluminosilicate Nanoparticles Enable Heterogeneous Activation of Endogenous Transforming Growth Factor β1 and Rapid Hemostasis for Bone Repair” by Chun Xu, Qingxuan Chen, Hang Chen, Aoni Xu, Juan Wen, Yiwei Li, Huan Dai, Siyuan Liu, Dan Cheng, Yaping Song, Bing Sun, Jie Tang, Jie Fan, Chang Lei and Chengzhong Yu, 15 September 2026, ACS Nano. DOI: 10.1021/acsnano.6c05126.

The authors acknowledge the funding support from Australian Research Council, National Health and Medical Research Council and the University of Sydney. A provisional patent application related to the findings reported in this manuscript has been filed by the University of Sydney and the University of Queensland. The application covers calcium-aluminosilicate mesoporous nanoparticles and their use for bone repair, as described in the paper (Provisional Patent Application No. 2026903515).

#54388. Does the Sun Have a Secret Companion? A Controversial Theory Could Explain Earth’s Mass Extinctions

Does the Sun Have a Secret Companion? A Controversial Theory Could Explain Earth’s Mass Extinctions

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mysterious 26-million-year pattern in Earth’s extinction history has fueled a controversial theory involving an unseen stellar companion to the Sun.
  • Scientists have long believed that long-period comets with highly inclined orbits, some capable of causing mass extinctions on Earth, originate in the hypothetical Oort Cloud.
  • Richard Muller, a well-known professor emeritus of physics at the University of California, Berkeley, has proposed another explanation for why some of these comets enter the inner solar system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mysterious 26-million-year pattern in Earth’s extinction history has fueled a controversial theory involving an unseen stellar companion to the Sun.

Scientists have long believed that long-period comets with highly inclined orbits, some capable of causing mass extinctions on Earth, originate in the hypothetical Oort Cloud. This vast, roughly spherical reservoir of icy bodies is thought to contain trillions of objects and extend as far as 1.6 light-years from the Sun.

Richard Muller, a well-known professor emeritus of physics at the University of California, Berkeley, has proposed another explanation for why some of these comets enter the inner solar system. In addition to gravitational disturbances caused by passing stars, he suggests that a low-mass red dwarf star (dubbed Nemesis) could periodically redirect comets toward the Sun. Under this hypothesis, Nemesis and the Sun orbit a shared center of gravity.

According to Muller, Nemesis follows a slightly elongated orbit that periodically brings it into regions of the Oort Cloud, where its gravity could disrupt the paths of billions of comets.

Recent findings suggest that muller explained in a phone interview that these encounters could trigger comet showers lasting roughly a million years. The greatest number of comets would be redirected into the inner solar system when Nemesis passes through the cloud’s densest regions.

It has been revealed that the proposed Nemesis star is not related to the hypothetical Planet X. It also differs from unrelated stars that occasionally pass near the solar system and gravitationally disturb the Oort Cloud, potentially sending numerous comets inward.

Unlike these unpredictable stellar encounters, the Nemesis hypothesis proposes a recurring cycle. Muller believes this mechanism could explain a pattern of impacts on Earth spanning approximately 250 million years.

It has been revealed that muller points to a 1982 study published in the journal Science by paleontologists David Raup and Jack Sepkoski. The researchers compiled an extensive record of marine extinctions that, according to Muller, revealed a striking pattern of extinction events occurring roughly every 26 million years.

The challenge was to come up with an explanation, says Muller. “Well, maybe there’s a companion star that comes close in to the Oort Cloud every 26 million years, and then triggers a comet hitting Earth,” he says.

It’s an idea that Muller still very much supports, although he isn’t sanguine about being able to directly observe Nemesis.

Despite what others seem to think, there is no clear evidence against this hypothesis, indicates Muller.

The Oort Cloud, a heretofore unseen, largely spherical cloud of comets and small icy bodies left over from the formation of our solar system some 4.5 billion years ago, very much remains a mystery.

There are three sources for the original material that formed the Oort Cloud, Astrophysicist Sean Raymond, Director of France’s Bordeaux Astrophysical Laboratory, told me via email.

Planetesimals that originated in our Sun’s planet-forming disk; planetesimals that originated around other stars in our Sun’s birth cluster, and interstellar objects that were captured during stellar encounters or by scattering by Jupiter, he notes.

According to recent reports, many astronomers assume that if Nemesis is an ordinary red dwarf, somebody would have seen it, and the answer is no, because it’s moving with the Sun around the center of gravity. And as a result, Nemesis doesn’t show enough proper motion, or movement across our line of sight, to be detectable.

But it must be big enough to perturb the Oort cloud, which means it’s probably at least five percent the mass of the Sun, notes Muller.

The consensus view is the K-T extinction event, which impacted the Yucatan Peninsula some 66 million years ago, was most likely caused by a large asteroid.

Industry observers note that yet the evidence that it’s an asteroid rather than a comet is very weak, so people say asteroid because that’s what Walter Alvarez, a professor of Earth and Planetary Science also at the University of California, Berkeley, said in his initial K-T Boundary paper, Muller notes. But when I asked Alvarez, I said, “You said asteroid. Could it be a comet?”.

He responded, “Sure, we couldn’t tell the difference.”.

The best near-term chance of characterizing this massive cloud, however, comes from the Rubin Observatory, which is just coming online. Astronomers hope that Rubin will be able to detect more long-period Oort Cloud comets.

The next comet shower that could cause serious damage to Earth should not be for another 12 to 15 million years from now, states Muller.

The bad news is that if it’s out there, Nemesis almost certainly would lie close to the plane of the ecliptic, which means that from our point of view, it would lie coplanar with most of the bodies of the outer solar system. And as a dim 8th or possibly 9th magnitude star, this would make it even more difficult to spot, certainly impossible to see with the naked eye.

So, Nemesis really is probably lost in a field of view that includes a huge number of other stars, states Muller.

Industry observers note that references: “Dynamical Population of Comet Reservoirs” by Nathan A. Kaib and Kathryn Volk, May 30, 2022, arXiv. DOI: 2206.00010.

Industry observers note that “Measurement of the lunar impact record for the past 3.5 b.y. and implications for the Nemesis theory” by Richard A. Muller, 01 January 2002, Geological Society of America DOI: 10.1130/0-8137-2356-6.659.

According to recent reports, “Mass Extinctions in the Marine Fossil Record” by David M. Raup and J. John Sepkoski, Jr., 19 March 1982, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.215.4539.1501.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that many fields of science have struggled under the second Trump administration, with funding cuts and delays plaguing research in fields such as public health and climate science. But some topics have found firmer footing, including artificial intelligence and quantum science.

According to recent reports, these technologies, along with supercomputing, “are going to be the three legs of the stool that is going to transform how science and engineering is done,” notes Darío Gil, undersecretary for science at the U.S. Department of Energy.

In November 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order to launch the Genesis Mission, a $5 billion whole-of-government effort to advance science via artificial intelligence. The initiative began with the DOE but has since expanded to more than 15 federal agencies.

It has been revealed that in June, the president issued an executive order that aims to accelerate the development of tools such as quantum computers, quantum sensors and quantum networks. And in July, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy issued a 123-page report describing its vision for a “golden age” of federal science, in which agencies align investments in research and development with administration priorities.

Federal agencies spent some $4.2 billion on AI R&D in 2025, according to an arm of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy that quantifies such investments.

Many scientists are enthusiastic about the opportunities for AI and quantum research. But some caution that a measured approach is needed. “My strongest opinion … is that I want to see all fields of science supported,” says Brad Marston, a physicist at Brown University and president of the American Physical Society. “Priorities have to be chosen, but getting a good balance is important, because you never know where some advance will come from.”.

Sources indicate that through Genesis, the DOE intends to use its troves of data as well as experimental and computing facilities to produce a common set of AI tools and a shared ecosystem for science. “That’s conceptually a very powerful idea,” claims astronomer Rachel Mandelbaum of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. “And if it pans out as intended, it could drive great advances in science and technology.”.

This year, DOE funded nearly 300 projects through Genesis — including one led by Mandelbaum. Her team’s effort aims to unify immense datasets from astronomical facilities around the world, such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument and the Zwicky Transient Facility. That would enable AI models to be trained on the data, which could help uncover hidden astronomical insights.

It has been revealed that H. Stockebrand/RubinObs/NOIRLab/AURA/SLAC/DOE/NSF.

Recent findings suggest that other projects include efforts to accelerate nuclear reactor development, create simulations of the U.S. electric grid and study nuclear fusion. And federal agencies including the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health have rolled out their own Genesis efforts, centered around the mission’s National Science and Technology Challenges, which include topics in health, biology, energy, space, national security and more.

It has been revealed that many scientists were already wielding AI in their work. But Genesis “really did create an inflection point,” states John Sarrao, director of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in Menlo Park, Calif. SLAC is now involved with 20 Genesis projects and leads two.

Compared with AI, quantum technologies are less mature. With quantum computing, “we’re still at mile one or two or three of a marathon,” states Celia Merzbacher, executive director of the Quantum Economic Development Consortium, a coalition of public and private institutions that works to bolster quantum tech in the United States. Nevertheless, researchers hope the two technologies can amplify one another. AI could help design and develop quantum computers, for example, while quantum computing demonstrates promise for efficiently tackling certain machine learning problems.

Recent findings suggest that accordingly, several Genesis projects involve quantum error correction, quantum sensors and quantum materials. And the DOE’s Quantum Genesis initiative aims to develop scientifically useful, error-corrected quantum computers by 2028.

Recent findings suggest that AI and quantum were not always hot topics. “Both of those areas … were kind of backwaters until recent advances,” Marston notes. Before the development of deep neural networks, for example, AI was mostly a curiosity. “It points to the importance of having a balanced approach to science funding,” he says. What starts as an obscure scientific specialty may suddenly explode into wide relevance.

It has been revealed that in the context of limited resources, prioritizing one area of research necessitates deprioritizing another. While some funding for the DOE’s portion of Genesis came from the One Major Beautiful Bill passed in 2025, much of the rest came from the DOE’s budget.

As excited as Mandelbaum is about Genesis, she is concerned about funding for non-AI related work. A cosmology grant her group received from the DOE didn’t align with Genesis mission priorities and was reduced this year, she says. “If the reality is that some of this [funding] is coming out of the baseline research budget in my field, then I think that it would be beneficial for the DOE to engage the scientific community about those trade-offs,” Mandelbaum says.

In response to these concerns, Gil states that the money going to Genesis from the DOE’s Office of Science — about $400 million so far — is small compared to the office’s total FY2026 budget of $8.4 billion.

In a recent development, sarrao claims that it’s crucial to build on the momentum of Genesis while still supporting the DOE’s core research. His impression is that things are trending in the right direction. “Are there really exciting opportunities? Yes, 100 percent,” Sarrao says. “Are there risks if you get the balance wrong? Equally well, 100 percent.”.

#54385. NASA Smashed Into an Asteroid. Now ESA’s Hera Spacecraft Is About to Reveal the Damage
