💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for more than 150 years, a burial found on the grounds of Westminster Abbey remained a mystery.
  • In a recent development, if you went only by the inscription carved on the limestone sarcophagus excavated on the North Green at Westminster Abbey in 1869, you’d understandably assume it held the remains of Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in Roman Britain around 300 C.E.
  • It certainly didn’t help that a written account in 1873 declared the skeleton lost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for more than 150 years, a burial found on the grounds of Westminster Abbey remained a mystery. Clues from the coffin itself, not to mention the skeleton inside, puzzled experts until Westminster Abbey’s consultant archaeologist, Warwick Rodwell, identified the deceased as a high-ranking medieval monk. He went one step further, determining the bones belonged to Aelfwig, an abbot of the Abbey’s Benedictine monastery, although Rodwell left open the possibility that the occupant was another abbot.

In a recent development, if you went only by the inscription carved on the limestone sarcophagus excavated on the North Green at Westminster Abbey in 1869, you’d understandably assume it held the remains of Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in Roman Britain around 300 C.E. Archaeological research isn’t that simple, though. A Latin cross dated to the 10th or 11th century was also carved across the lid, likely when the coffin was reused, so with conflicting symbology muddying the waters, the identity of the person entombed on the Abbey’s grounds remained unknown for generations.

It certainly didn’t help that a written account in 1873 declared the skeleton lost. In 2016, however, conservators found the bones where they had presumably been all along: inside the coffin.

Rodwell worked on the puzzle for years, eventually publishing a study in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association explaining how the evidence led him to two abbots who served at the monastery. His first candidate, Aelfwig, died around 1020, but the second option was Aelfwig’s successor, Wulfnoth, who died 29 years later.

“We have two viable contenders for the occupant of the sarcophagus,” Rodwell stated in a statement from the Abbey. He ruled out Aelfwig’s predecessor because that abbot left the area and died elsewhere. “We do not know the date of birth of either. But either would fit equally well if we assume the abbot was in his early 20s when the appointment was made and close to 50 when he died. The fact Aelfwig was already a monk of Westminster might favor him.”.

The sarcophagus’s own history reveals little. The limestone probably came from Oxfordshire, England. But Rodwell wrote that no clues link the sarcophagus to its original burial site or explain why it was later moved, even though the inscription clearly ties it to a Briton who lived about 1,700 years ago. Identification is further complicated by the Anglo-Saxon cross added to the lid centuries later and by Rodwell’s belief that grave goods were stolen in the early 19th century.

To learn more about the man himself, Rodwell worked with James Young Langhorne, a human bone specialist from Pre-Construct Archaeology. They determined that the man was between 35 and 49 years old and stood about 5 feet, 9 inches tall. That contradicts the 19th-century assessment, which described him as a “robust young man” no older than 30 and about 5 feet, 7 inches tall. The analysis also showed osteoarthritis in multiple joints, two healed rib fractures, and signs of an old infection in one leg. There was no obvious cause of death.

Radiocarbon dating by the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre placed the bones between 987 and 1052 C.E. This confirmed that the sarcophagus had been reused, and the date range matches the Saxon-period cross on the lid. With that range established, Rodwell looked more closely at the possible candidates.

He concluded the man was an abbot because he was “honored” with burial in a “fine sarcophagus”: his wooden coffin was packed in lime and placed inside the stone casket. To support his theory further, Rodwell wrote that he believes the “prestigious burial” first took place in the eastern arm of the abbey church. The sarcophagus would have been fully buried, with the recut lid serving as a cross-slab in the church floor. Then, after Henry III began rebuilding the abbey in the 1240s, workers moved the sarcophagus into the “newly constructed sacristy courtyard” in 1258.

Today, the sarcophagus is on permanent display in the Abbey’s museum, The Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Galleries.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. You Can Build All the Power Plants You Want. Without This Overlooked Machine, None of Them Will Matter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As humanity entered the 21st century and the ravages of climate change became more and more apparent, the push toward electrification (replacing gas-powered cars, furnaces, and stoves with electric versions) really gained steam.
  • Industry observers note that but building out an electrified future isn’t as easy as sticking wind turbines in the ocean and vast solar arrays in the desert and calling it a day.
  • In a new study published in the journal Cell Reports Sustainability, researchers at Johns Hopkins University report that critical grid equipment, such as transformers and converters, could become the bottleneck in powering a rapidly electrifying society.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As humanity entered the 21st century and the ravages of climate change became more and more apparent, the push toward electrification (replacing gas-powered cars, furnaces, and stoves with electric versions) really gained steam. At the same time, the electricity supply itself has been getting cleaner. According to Pew Research, solar power accounted for only 0.01 percent of the world’s electricity production back then, but fast-forward a quarter of a century, and that number is now nine percent and rising.

Industry observers note that but building out an electrified future isn’t as easy as sticking wind turbines in the ocean and vast solar arrays in the desert and calling it a day. These upcoming forms of renewable energy also need to connect to the grid before they can supply us with that much-needed new power. Expanding the grid’s capacity to meet this ballooning demand was already going to be a tall order as more and more electric cars, ovens, and heat pumps came online. Now, the rise of power-hungry AI data centers has transformed that difficult task into a borderline impossible one for the simple reason that the U.S. may not have enough of the equipment—or the materials to make said equipment—to build the required infrastructure.

In a new study published in the journal Cell Reports Sustainability, researchers at Johns Hopkins University report that critical grid equipment, such as transformers and converters, could become the bottleneck in powering a rapidly electrifying society. According to the researchers, demand for electricity isn’t anything new. In fact, it’s been steadily rising since Thomas Edison flipped the switch on the Pearl Street Station in 1882. But due to the rise of AI data centers, the electricity industry has entered a whole new era of demand growth.

“When the demand for electricity started to grow faster than expected, it started to amplify all the cracks in the industry,” Yury Dvorkin, a Johns Hopkins researcher and co-author of the study, mentioned in a press statement. According to Dvorkin and co-author Boyu Yao, electricity demand historically ticked up a percent or two each year. But now, largely because of data centers, demand is projected to grow 21 percent overall by the end of the decade.

If this rapid demand growth persists, it will put considerable strain on supplies of specific materials, including copper, steel, nickel, aluminum, and manganese, needed to build the necessary transformers, which step up or step down the voltage of alternating current on the grid.

“This type of equipment was taken for granted, but without it, you can build a data center or a power plant but it won’t be powered because you cannot connect it to the grid,” Dvorkin said. “By 2030 we’re likely to have transformer shortages even without the most aggressive power demand growth.”.

It has been revealed that according to their projections, copper will run short in 2027, followed soon by steel and nickel, which will affect not just grid utilities but wind power infrastructure and electric vehicle charging stations. This shortfall isn’t necessarily news: a study by S&P Global earlier this year found that copper could experience a 10 million metric ton deficit by 2040. This deficit isn’t caused by a lack of copper in the ground, since the planet holds abundant copper resources. Extraction is where the industry is facing a crucial bottleneck.

According to recent reports, “Copper is abundant in the ground, but there’s not enough being extracted to be able to meet the demand,” authors of a copper market analysis wrote for The Conversation earlier this year. That’s because investors want higher and more reliable returns than copper mines presently offer, and the industry faces complex permitting processes and can’t find enough workers.

This new study suggests that under its baseline scenario, the U.S. might be able to produce enough transformers yet still fall 16 percent short on other grid-related equipment. But with AI data centers supercharging demand, the study’s “high power demand” scenario is more likely. That scenario projects a 15 percent shortage of transformers and a 30 percent shortage of all other equipment. The authors also note that roughly two-thirds of this expected shortage can be attributed to AI data centers.

According to recent reports, “Utilities will compete for transformers with the data center industry,” Dvorkin mentioned. “Transformers will first be delivered to whoever can pay the highest premium. Will it be a mom-and-pop utility or a massive data center corporation?”.

I think we already know the answer to that question.

  • Industry observers note that in work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Recent findings suggest that for seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter. It swelled to more than twice its original size, even as its surface temperature barely changed. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. The slow brightening and sudden eruption tell a story of a smaller star orbiting inside of a massive star and what became of the pair, researchers report November 18 in Nature.

Industry observers note that in work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers. Astronomers call this elusive phase of a binary star’s life common-envelope evolution.

Now, the astronomers have analyzed the system’s dramatic next developments, culminating in the October 2025 eruption. (The stars are nicknamed Little Bao and Big Bao as a nod to that event’s official designation, AT 2025abao.).

First, astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University and colleagues revisited those years of brightening given the imminent eruption. One cause of the brightening could have been gas flowing away from the stars, giving off light as it slowed down. But even if all the energy of that moving gas turned into light, it still wouldn’t be enough to explain the glow.

Sources indicate that instead, the researchers determined that the binary hypothesis they had originally proposed fit better: As Little Bao orbited inside Big Bao’s gas outer layers, the gas pushed back against the little star. That drag made Little Bao spiral inward and transfer energy to the surrounding gas. Some of that energy escaped as light, making Big Bao shine brighter.

Industry observers note that then, it was time to dig into what caused the eruption. If the outburst threw enough of the shared gas into space, the individual stars could have survived in an even tighter orbit. But the team estimates that only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped. The energy carried by that fast-moving gas also suggests that Little Bao reached Major Bao’s core. Together, those clues point to a merger.

Industry observers note that still, too much dust clouds the system to directly see what remains. And it won’t settle for years or even decades, although Karambelkar and his colleagues will be watching.

They’ll be looking for more examples of this type of merger, too. “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems,” Karambelkar says, “and hopefully aim to catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”.

Industry News: Meet the Planimal: Half Hamster Cell, Half Algae, 100% Weird

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Almost all of the major events that changed the trajectory of life on Earth had impossibly tiny beginnings, and the rise of plant life is no exception.
  • Despite the vast evolutionary gulf between them (the two lineages diverged in the middle of the Proterozoic Eon), a new study published in the journal Nature Communications suggests that the cells derived from red algae and mammals still have the capacity to acquire genetic material through a process known as “horizontal gene transfer.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Almost all of the major events that changed the trajectory of life on Earth had impossibly tiny beginnings, and the rise of plant life is no exception. Some 1.5 billion years ago, a eukaryotic cell engulfed a cyanobacterium, which eventually evolved into the chloroplast, the specialized organelle that drives photosynthesis in algae and plants. Other eukaryotic cells, of course, took a very different path, giving rise to all animals and, ultimately, the mammalian cells that make up you and me.

Despite the vast evolutionary gulf between them (the two lineages diverged in the middle of the Proterozoic Eon), a new study published in the journal Nature Communications suggests that the cells derived from red algae and mammals still have the capacity to acquire genetic material through a process known as “horizontal gene transfer.”.

Obviously, most gene transfers in nature move from parents to offspring (fittingly named “vertical gene transfer”), but sometimes cells will acquire traits from other individuals, strains, or even entire species. This is seen most commonly in bacteria that share antibiotic resistance genes, or ARGs, creating troublesome antimicrobial-resistant (or drug-resistant) superbugs in the process. However, other fascinating examples exist, including a parasitic worm that can control its host by swapping genes. In their new study, a team of scientists led by researchers at the University of Tokyo explored whether a similar process could take place between cells separated by more than a billion years of evolution, resulting in what the researchers call “planimal” cells.

“We wanted to understand whether entire chromosomes could cross the enormous evolutionary divide between algae and animals and whether animal cells could stably maintain and pass on such foreign genetic material to their daughter cells,” University of Tokyo biologist Sachihiro Matsunaga, senior author of the study, stated in a press statement. “These questions are fundamental to understanding how genetic material can move across species boundaries and contribute to evolution.”.

To investigate this possibility, the authors relied on cells derived from the red alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae, along with mammal cells originating from a hamster. Mirroring the primordial event that gave rise to plant life, the researchers allowed the mammalian cell to engulf the alga, after which—surprisingly—cell fusion produced stable hybrid cells. Armed with advanced imaging and genome sequencing, Matsunaga and his team could track how well host mammalian cells retained this algal DNA over subsequent generations. They found that 16.3 million algal base pairs and intact chromosome sequences from all 20 algal chromosomes were retained, and the algal DNA remained detectable through 155 cell generations.

In a recent development, “Plants and animals cannot reproduce with each other, so their chromosomes are never combined through mating. Yet, we have succeeded in creating hybrid chromosomes containing genetic material from both an alga and a mammal,” Matsunaga noted. “This demonstrates that even the vast evolutionary divide between plants and animals can be crossed at the level of chromosomes, without reproduction.”.

The key to the planimal cells’ survival was the epigenetic “gatekeeping” ability of the host cell to essentially silence incorporated foreign DNA. The authors estimate that roughly 96 percent of the algal protein-coding genes were basically offline, but it’s possible that future studies could detect how to flip this gene switch to “on.”.

“Our ultimate goal is to activate these biological pathways and give animal cells some of the unique abilities of plants and algae,” Matsunaga added. “Imagine animal cells that could sustain photosynthesis for long periods, producing oxygen while using carbon dioxide to make useful organic compounds.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.
  • Industry observers note that sources said Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Industry observers note that sources said Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Sources indicate that senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”.

The post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

In a recent development, paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”.

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

It has been revealed that in 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

In a recent development, after Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

According to recent reports, clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

It has been revealed that “The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker said. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”.

It has been revealed that walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Sources indicate that over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this key position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

In a recent development, the Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Recent findings suggest that collins stated in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”.

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

#54357. Tech Report: Why researchers are paying attention to the jolt you feel just as you drift off

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (980 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Why researchers are paying attention to the jolt you feel just as you drift off

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (980 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest survey links frequent sleep starts, the sudden jolts that can happen as you drift off, to poorer sleep, more severe insomnia, and greater anxiety.
  • Most people have felt it: the sudden jerk as sleep arrives, a leg kick or a whole-body twitch, sometimes with a falling feeling that snaps the eyes open.
  • In a upcoming survey, people who reported weekly sleep starts along with at least one other symptom reported poorer sleep than those who rarely or never had them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest survey links frequent sleep starts, the sudden jolts that can happen as you drift off, to poorer sleep, more severe insomnia, and greater anxiety.

Most people have felt it: the sudden jerk as sleep arrives, a leg kick or a whole-body twitch, sometimes with a falling feeling that snaps the eyes open.

In a upcoming survey, people who reported weekly sleep starts along with at least one other symptom reported poorer sleep than those who rarely or never had them.

They also report worse insomnia, more unhelpful beliefs about sleep, and more anxiety.

The survey was online and the answers were self-reported, so it can show a pattern and not a cause. The authors wrote that the jolts and the worry may feed each other, but their data can’t say which comes first.

Tanja Grünberger and Manuel Schabus of the University of Salzburg in Austria led the work with colleagues there.

Sleep researchers call the jolt a hypnic jerk or a sleep start.

Recent findings suggest that studies that have wired people up while they doze put it in the drowsy stretch between waking and light sleep. The recordings show a brief burst of muscle activity and often a faster heartbeat.

Recent findings suggest that the 96 people in the survey who had sleep starts weekly described far more than a twitch. Muscle jerks were the most common feature, reported by 87.5%.

About two-thirds described a sensation of falling or losing balance, and about the same share reported tingling or numbness.

Nearly half had felt something like an electric shock, 47.9% had seen flashes with their eyes closed, and 21.9% had heard a loud bang that wasn’t there.

Dream-like images, often of falling, went with the jolt for 74%.

It has been revealed that the feelings that came with the jolt were mostly unpleasant. Alarm and confusion followed for about four in five participants, and panic for 71.9%. Even so, 95.8% said they usually fell back asleep promptly.

According to recent reports, the researchers recruited 194 adults in Austria and Germany, mostly women, with an average age of about 33. Anyone reporting restless legs, sleep apnea, epilepsy or similar conditions was left out.

According to recent reports, ninety-six of them reported jolting awake at least weekly plus at least one other symptom. The other 98 served as the comparison group.

On standard questionnaires, the weekly group scored worse on sleep quality and on insomnia severity.

They held stronger unhelpful beliefs about sleep, rated sleep as more important to them, and scored higher on anxiety and depression.

The weekly group also took longer to fall asleep and slept slightly less.

Daytime sleepiness was the one measure that did not differ between the groups.

Within the weekly group, the people who jolted most often were the ones with the poorest sleep quality, the strongest unhelpful beliefs about sleep, and the most anxiety.

Depression scores were not linked to how often the jolts came.

Together, sleep quality, sleep beliefs, anxiety, age and gender accounted for about 27% of the differences in how often people reported sleep starts. Younger people reported them more often.

Industry observers note that asked what made the jolts more frequent, participants pointed to stress, tension and emotional strain. Sleep loss came up less often.

“The more strongly participants held unhelpful beliefs about sleep and the more anxious they were, the more often they reported sleep starts – and in the moment itself, many described a strong pressure to finally fall asleep,” Grünberger noted.

“Our data cannot show what causes what, but this pattern resembles what we know from insomnia.”.

The pressure to sleep demonstrated up in the numbers. Among the weekly group, 83.3% noted the thought “I finally have to sleep!” ran through their heads around the jolt, and 76% said they had tried to force themselves back to sleep.

Sources indicate that just over half of those with weekly jolts said the episodes made it harder to fall asleep. Among those who reported a delay, it averaged about 43 minutes. About 41% said the jolts made no difference.

The authors read the pattern against a well-known idea in insomnia research: the harder a person monitors and strains for sleep, the more alert they become.

In that view, the jolt and the worry about the jolt can keep each other going.

To calm the jolts, participants most often tried steering their thoughts elsewhere at bedtime, relaxation exercises, exercise, and cutting noise and light in the bedroom. They rated those as only modestly helpful.

There is no standard questionnaire for sleep starts, so the team wrote its own items from the clinical literature.

The questions have not been tested against any validated measure, and the weekly cutoff that defined the groups was chosen after the data were in.

The survey also could not separate sleep starts from look-alike experiences, such as the loud-noise phenomenon called exploding head syndrome or vivid images as sleep begins.

People answered from memory, and no one’s sleep was recorded in a lab.

“Because there is no established questionnaire for sleep starts, we developed our own items based on the clinical literature,” Grünberger mentioned.

“This allowed us to capture a broad range of experiences – but it also means that our findings now need to be confirmed with validated instruments and objective sleep recordings.”.

In a recent development, the next step, Schabus said, is to test whether treatments that lower arousal and sleep worry, the kind used for insomnia, also ease distressing sleep starts. No one has run that test yet.

Until someone does, the survey offers a description of the jolt and the people it troubles, and an untested idea about why.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Mental Health.

Fatal cases of Ebola often share a striking pattern

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ebola may trap immune messages inside infected cells, keeping the body's defenses active longer and potentially worsening illness.
  • A deadly virus such as Ebola might be expected to kill by shutting down the body’s defenses.
  • Industry observers note that ebola virus does make proteins that block a key signal the body uses to fight infection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ebola may trap immune messages inside infected cells, keeping the body's defenses active longer and potentially worsening illness.

A deadly virus such as Ebola might be expected to kill by shutting down the body’s defenses.

Industry observers note that ebola virus does make proteins that block a key signal the body uses to fight infection. The pattern in patients, however, is the opposite.

People who die from Ebola often show the highest activity in the genes that fight viruses.

Scientists have struggled to explain this for years.

A new study points to the tiny droplets of protein and RNA that Ebola virus builds inside infected cells. These droplets are known as viral condensates, and the cell’s own immune messages become trapped inside them.

Once trapped, the messages are not broken down when they should be.

The defense therefore remains switched on. That prolonged response may be part of what makes patients so ill.

The findings come during a major outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

As of November 17, the CDC reported 11,613 confirmed cases and 5,678 confirmed deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The outbreak involves Bundibugyo virus, a close relative of the virus studied here.

Seven genes is all Ebola virus carries.

Industry observers note that two of them make proteins called NP and VP35. Both attach to viral RNA and to each other, gathering into droplets that have no outer membrane.

During an infection they can take up between one-fifth and one-third of a cell.

Jingru Fang led the work in the Saphire Lab at the La Jolla Institute for Immunology. Fang now works at Princeton University’s Omenn-Darling Bioengineering Institute.

“When birds land in a new place, they make nests where they can raise their babies,” mentioned Fang.

“You can imagine viral condensates as nests for a virus.”.

Recent findings suggest that to study the droplets, NP and VP35 were introduced into human kidney cells. The actual virus was left out, and the droplets still formed.

The messenger RNA in those cells was then stained. Messenger RNA carries the instructions a cell uses to make a protein.

Messenger RNA was more concentrated inside the droplets than in the surrounding cell fluid.

Industry observers note that in human cells, the buildup came to roughly 40%. Kidney cells from Egyptian fruit bats showed an even greater buildup.

When NP was changed so that it could no longer attach to single-stranded RNA, that buildup fell by about half.

In a recent development, A similar change to VP35 had little effect in human cells. NP appears to play the bigger role in collecting RNA.

That figure covers every message at once, and says nothing about which ones are collected.

The team therefore used a method capable of reading thousands of RNA types at once, across 136 genes linked to Ebola infection and the immune response.

About 90,000 cells were examined, with droplets found in roughly 30% of them. Of the 66 genes measured reliably, all but two were more concentrated inside.

Sources indicate that the amount of RNA made little difference. Rare messages collected inside while far more common ones stayed out, indicating that something other than abundance determined where they ended up.

Shape proved to be the better explanation.

RNA is not always a straight strand. Parts of it join together wherever the letters match, folding the molecule into loops and stems.

Messages with fewer folds in their protein-making sections entered more readily.

To test this, the genetic instructions in some messages were rewritten. The upcoming versions made the same protein but folded differently, and those with fewer folds entered more readily.

Ten viruses that carry negative-strand RNA were also examined, including Ebola, measles, rabies and Marburg. In all of them the protein-making regions had fewer folds than the human messages left outside.

Industry observers note that the most striking finding concerned interferon. Type I interferon, released when a cell detects a virus, switches on hundreds of defense genes in nearby cells.

After the cells were treated with interferon, the droplets started collecting different messages.

Messages from more than 20 defense genes appeared in droplets.

According to recent reports, the rule governing entry also changed. The protein-making section was no longer the best indicator.

Instead the tail of each message mattered more, the stretch that follows the instructions for making a protein.

Immune defense messages often have long, tightly folded tails.

According to recent reports, the more folded the tail, the more of that message was found inside. Interferon also increases proteins that attach to RNA, and some of these may help pull immune messages into the droplets.

In a recent development, people who die from Ebola often show stronger activity in their defense genes than those who survive. Even people who recover can show signs of inflammation-related gene activity years later.

Erica Ollmann Saphire, who led the study with Fang, is the president and chief executive of the La Jolla Institute for Immunology.

“These are strong immune responses, but they’re not working well,” said Ollmann Saphire.

According to recent reports, cells normally break down messenger RNA once it has served its purpose. Enzymes such as XRN1 help carry out that cleanup.

Staining indicated less XRN1 inside the droplets than in the surrounding cell fluid.

This raised a further question: whether messages trapped inside survive longer because the enzymes cannot reach them.

Messages held in the droplets broke down more slowly than the same messages in cells carrying a modified NP that could not bind RNA. Messages that stayed outside broke down at similar rates in both groups.

“The antiviral response is like a weapon, and cells use degradation as a way to deactivate that weapon,” Fang explained.

Industry observers note that protein production also changed. A protein the cell requires in order to start building other proteins was largely missing from the droplets.

Without interferon, more messenger RNA collected inside but less protein came out of it.

With interferon, both rose: one defense message increased more than sixfold, and levels of two defense proteins rose alongside it.

A final experiment used a weakened Ebola virus, one lacking a gene needed for replication.

A defense message called IFIT3 was found inside the droplets of those infected cells as well.

Bats can carry filoviruses without getting sick. These viruses belong to the same family as Ebola.

It has been revealed that bat genes cannot be read with tools designed for human RNA. Computer models were therefore used to predict how 45 of the collected messages would fold, in bats, ferrets and macaques.

Ferrets and macaques can become seriously ill from Ebola, which makes them useful comparisons.

According to recent reports, within the defense genes, the bat versions had tails that were less tightly folded than the human ones. Ferret and macaque tails were much more like those in humans.

Genes outside the defense group revealed no meaningful difference between species.

Fever often comes with an interferon response, so the predictions were repeated at 102 degrees Fahrenheit (39 degrees Celsius).

Recent findings suggest that messages carrying bat tails then behaved as the folding had predicted. The least folded bat tail kept its message out of the droplets better than the matching human tail.

Bat immune messages may therefore be less likely to become trapped. If they remain outside, cells can break them down at the usual time.

Sources indicate that most experiments used kidney cells grown in a laboratory. The process was not tested in human patients or living animals, and for much of the work NP and VP35 stood in for the complete virus.

The cells were measured at just one point, 24 hours after the proteins were introduced, across 136 genes out of roughly 20,000.

The human kidney cells responded poorly to interferon. Higher concentrations were therefore used for longer periods than other tissues might need.

In a recent development, the RNA folding patterns were computer predictions. They cannot fully show how every RNA molecule behaves inside a living cell.

Sources indicate that the bat comparison included only one species. It was chosen partly because scientists have not yet identified Ebola virus’s natural host.

“We don’t know whether this difference can explain everything, but it gives researchers a place to start looking and confirm what we’ve found in additional human or animal samples,” Fang added.

Industry observers note that breaking the droplets apart may be worth pursuing as a treatment, the authors wrote. It could slow the virus and prevent immune messages from remaining active too long.

The principal challenge is achieving that inside living cells without destroying the cells.

The full study was published in the journal Cell.

A rose-colored rock found in the Sahara turned out to be a 4.1-billion-year-old piece of Mars

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (869 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 4.1-billion-year-old Martian meteorite found in Mali's Sahara Desert reveals clues about ancient crust, water activity and Mars' early history.
  • A rose-colored meteorite found in the Sahara Desert formed on Mars at least 4.1 billion years ago, a study published October 29, 2026, reports.
  • Named Teghaza 001 after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered, it is one of roughly 435 known meteorites from Mars, NASA states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 4.1-billion-year-old Martian meteorite found in Mali's Sahara Desert reveals clues about ancient crust, water activity and Mars' early history.

A rose-colored meteorite found in the Sahara Desert formed on Mars at least 4.1 billion years ago, a study published October 29, 2026, reports.

Named Teghaza 001 after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered, it is one of roughly 435 known meteorites from Mars, NASA states. It is also one of the three most ancient Martian meteorites found on Earth.

Its composition, mineralogy and texture are distinct from those of other Martian meteorites.

Meteorite hunters found eight stones at the beginning of September 2022, weighing nearly 1.8 pounds (798.5 grams) in total.

The largest weighs about 15.6 ounces (442 grams), the Meteoritical Bulletin, the official record of named meteorites, demonstrates.

In a recent development, the stones had no fusion crust, the glassy skin that forms during a fall. Their surfaces were sandblasted, and the largest pieces carried mineral coatings from burial in the desert.

At first, Teghaza 001 appeared to be a shergottite, the most common class of meteorite from Mars. It is about 50 percent pyroxene and 40 percent maskelynite, a glass formed when an impact shocks plagioclase feldspar.

Many of its pyroxene crystals have cores with thin layers of iron and manganese oxides, a product of alteration.

Oxygen isotope measurements at the University of New Mexico (UNM), which holds a 0.8-ounce (22-gram) type specimen, matched known Martian meteorites. Carl Agee, director and curator of UNM’s Institute of Meteoritics and a co-author of the study, classified the rock.

“This is just one single meteorite. It’s like going out back in time and chipping off a hunk of an outcrop,” Agee mentioned.

The lead author, Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, and her colleagues found tiny zircon crystals in the rock. Such crystals allow scientists to date igneous rocks with uranium-lead measurements.

Industry observers note that A second method, in-situ rubidium-strontium dating, analyzed single mineral grains on a piece of the meteorite smaller than a fingernail. Further analysis revealed when the rock formed and when changes such as water alteration occurred.

The team describes Teghaza 001 as a slowly cooled igneous rock and a sample of ancient crust. That crust formed from a geochemically distinct mantle source with a primordial composition.

“It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique,” Liu mentioned.

Its exact origin can never be known for sure, but features of the rock link it to highlands in the southern hemisphere of Mars. Using data from NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, the researchers identified 13 locations whose mineralogy and chemistry match it.

“This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before,” remarked Lee Saper, the second author.

Saper did the research as a postdoctoral scholar at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and now works at NASA’s Ames Research Center.

According to recent reports, most Martian meteorites are roughly 200 million years old, according to UNM. NASA says the two other ancient ones give more limited glimpses of Mars’ geological history.

One is ALH84001, discovered in 1984 and composed almost entirely of one mineral.

According to recent reports, A University of Houston team used lutetium-hafnium isotopes in 2010 to date it to 4.091 billion years, about 400 million years younger than earlier estimates. That age is similar to Teghaza 001’s.

The other, nicknamed “Black Beauty,” formed about 2.1 billion years ago and is made of small, volcanic rock fragments. Some of the minerals inside it are far older.

They include a 4.45 billion-year-old zircon. Scientists at Curtin University have reported that this grain preserves evidence of damage that only occurs during large meteorite impacts.

“I realized that this one was a little bit like Black Beauty, not exactly, but it resembled it in the oxygen isotope values,” Agee stated of Teghaza 001.

Teghaza 001’s water-altered minerals and oxygen isotopes indicate that it reacted with fluids enriched in oxygen-18 before an impact blasted it into space. Some fine-grained carbonate, sulfate and clay minerals in the rock formed later, on Earth.

In a recent development, martian water altered the rock sometime around 4.1 billion years ago, which suggests it formed even earlier, NASA stated. Clues in its oxygen isotopes, texture and chemistry point to a much more dynamic water cycle on early Mars.

A June 2026 study of its water, led by Saper, had already reported the meteorite’s age and identified it as a gabbroic diorite.

Hydrogen isotopes in its phosphate minerals suggest that Martian water then held at least about twice as much deuterium, relative to hydrogen, as Earth’s seawater.

That minimum value supports models in which hydrogen escaped rapidly to space from Mars’ young atmosphere.

UNM ties the rock to the Pre-Noachian, the period from about 4.5 billion to 4.1 billion years ago.

In the Noachian that followed, until 3.7 billion years ago, groundwater chemically altered many rocks into clays, the European Space Agency notes.

The study was published in the journal Science.

#54352. Even slightly warmer summers are linked to a higher death risk for people with heart disease

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1449 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Even slightly warmer summers are linked to a higher death risk for people with heart disease

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1449 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A UK study links extreme heat and repeated heatwaves to higher death risks among people with heart disease.
  • In a recent development, an average summer temperature of about 62°F (16.5°C) sounds mild.
  • In a large UK study, researchers found that for every 1.8°F (1°C) increase in average summer temperature, patients had a 15% higher risk of dying from any cause.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A UK study links extreme heat and repeated heatwaves to higher death risks among people with heart disease.

In a recent development, an average summer temperature of about 62°F (16.5°C) sounds mild. But even slightly warmer summers were linked to a higher risk of death among people with cardiovascular disease.

In a large UK study, researchers found that for every 1.8°F (1°C) increase in average summer temperature, patients had a 15% higher risk of dying from any cause.

Industry observers note that the risk was also higher among patients who experienced more heat waves. The odds of death rose on the hottest days and after sharp jumps in temperature from one day to the next.

Taken together, the findings indicate that heat may influence survival across entire seasons in heart patients. An influence during brief hot spells is suggested as well.

According to recent reports, the research was conducted by Ka Yan Lai of the University of Hong Kong alongside colleagues there. Further collaborators were based at the University of Oxford.

Using health records, the investigators followed nearly 64,000 UK patients for periods of up to 16 years.

Lai mentioned the health effects of extreme heat have “rarely been studied among people with pre-existing conditions.”.

It has been revealed that all of the patients had been enrolled in UK Biobank, a long-running British health project. Half a million volunteers aged between 37 and 73 were recruited to it from 2006 to 2010.

From this pool, 63,860 volunteers were selected by the team for analysis.

All received their first hospital diagnosis of cardiovascular disease between 2006 and 2022.

Cardiovascular disease, or CVD, includes conditions that affect the heart and blood vessels.

Recent findings suggest that four of those disorders were examined on their own as well. Atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat, was the first of them.

In a recent development, the second was ischemic heart disease, in which narrowed arteries can’t deliver enough blood to the heart. Heart failure and stroke made up the remaining two.

It has been revealed that at diagnosis, the patients had reached an average age of about 69 years. Deaths from any cause had been recorded for 12,237 of them by the end of 2022.

That figure corresponds to roughly one patient in five.

Sources indicate that temperature data were taken from the daily records kept by the Met Office. Those records are mapped onto squares measuring about 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) across.

For every summer, defined as June through August, each home address was matched to its square.

Considerable variation in average summer temperature was evident across that map. The coldest squares averaged about 43°F (6.1°C), whereas the warmest reached about 66°F (18.7°C).

In a recent development, the central result relates to the average summer temperature at each patient’s place of residence. A 15% higher risk of death was associated with every additional 1.8°F (1°C).

Industry observers note that several other influences had been accounted for before that estimate was produced. Among them were age, sex, smoking, alcohol use, diabetes and neighborhood deprivation.

For patients with ischemic heart disease, each added degree Celsius corresponded to a 19% higher risk. A smaller increase of 10% was found among those with atrial fibrillation.

The results for heart failure and stroke were less certain. In both groups, the link with average summer temperature was too weak to exclude chance.

Adults aged 65 and older in New England had been examined in an earlier US study.

Recent findings suggest that A 1% increase in deaths was reported there for each 1.8°F (1°C) rise in long-term average summer temperature. Older adults in general were covered by that work, not only people with heart disease.

Heat waves were also counted by the researchers. A heat wave was defined as two or more consecutive days hotter than 90% of local summer days.

Recent findings suggest that exposure to four or more heat waves a year was experienced by some patients. Their risk of death exceeded by 24% that of patients exposed to two or fewer.

Among patients with atrial fibrillation, the corresponding increase in risk was 29%. It stood at 28% among those with heart failure.

A second analysis was restricted to patients whose deaths occurred during a summer.

For each such patient, temperatures on the day of death and the five preceding days were examined. These were then compared with other days in the same month that fell on the same weekday.

Because every patient served as their own comparison, fixed traits can’t account for the results. Sex and schooling are examples of such traits.

On the hottest 1% of summer days, the odds of death among the patients as a group were 70% higher. The reference point was the temperature at which deaths were lowest.

Temperature changes from one day to the next were measured as well. The largest one-day rises were taken to be those in the top 1% of such changes.

After rises of that size, the odds of death were roughly double those seen when temperature held constant.

Roughly threefold odds were found in patients with ischemic heart disease or heart failure.

Considerable uncertainty surrounds the estimates for sharp rises. In heart failure, the plausible range extended from 36% higher odds to more than seven times as high.

No clear link with deaths was detected for sudden drops in temperature.

According to recent reports, events inside the patients’ bodies were not measured at any point in the study. A plausible explanation was instead drawn by the authors from earlier research on extreme heat.

It has been revealed that in hot weather, warm blood is pumped toward the skin so that heat can be shed by the body. As much as 5 gallons (20 liters) of blood may be pumped by the heart each minute.

Sweating can meanwhile strip water and salt from the body. Blood that holds less water becomes thicker, and thicker blood may clot more readily.

In a person with heart disease, the extra pumping may require more oxygen than the heart can obtain.

Among patients lacking a college or university degree, warmer summers were tied more strongly to death. A weaker link was seen in patients who held such a degree.

A similar contrast emerged between neighborhoods with moderate green space and the greenest neighborhoods, where the link was weaker.

Among heart failure patients, the link was stronger in the most deprived neighborhoods.

It has been revealed that several possible reasons were put forward by the authors. Deprived neighborhoods tend to be overcrowded and to suffer more air pollution and traffic noise, they wrote.

Physically demanding work in extreme weather is also more common among people with less money.

Green spaces, meanwhile, have been shown in earlier studies to cool their surroundings.

In a recent development, according to Lai, protection will have to be delivered at several levels at once. City planning was named as one of those levels.

In a recent development, cooling strategies form another, as do personal decisions about where to live. Lai said such protection is needed most by the most vulnerable groups.

In a recent development, extreme heat is projected to grow more frequent and more intense as populations age. That observation came from study co-author Chinmoy Sarkar of the University of Hong Kong.

Together, he said, those trends will make protecting frail people with chronic diseases a top public health priority.

It has been revealed that A link between heat and death can be demonstrated by a study of this kind. Proof that heat caused the deaths lies beyond its reach.

In a recent development, because temperatures were assigned by home address, the patients’ actual whereabouts each day remain unrecorded. Nor was any information available on air-conditioning use or on changes in medication.

Smoking and drinking habits were recorded only once, when volunteers joined UK Biobank.

Those habits may well have changed afterward. Since cases were identified through hospital admissions, milder disease that never led to admission was missed.

It has been revealed that UK Biobank volunteers may also differ from the wider population. About 96% of the patients in this study were white. The authors wrote that the volunteers may not represent everyone in the UK with cardiovascular disease.

None of the patients was given a cooler home or a greener street during the study. How many deaths such changes might prevent therefore can’t be read from the records.

Air-conditioning use could be accounted for in future research, as could travel to places with different temperatures.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Climate.

Ice baths after exercise: What happens when you make them a habit?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ice baths may ease soreness after a hard workout, but regular cold plunges after lifting may limit gains in muscle size and strength.
  • An ice bath after a hard workout may ease muscle soreness.
  • A major review led by Edith Cowan University (ECU) found it can blunt long-term strength and muscle gains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ice baths may ease soreness after a hard workout, but regular cold plunges after lifting may limit gains in muscle size and strength.

An ice bath after a hard workout may ease muscle soreness. But taking one after every lifting session may make it harder to build muscle and strength over time.

A major review led by Edith Cowan University (ECU) found it can blunt long-term strength and muscle gains.

According to recent reports, researchers analyzed 15 published systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Together they covered 161 studies and more than 3,200 participants.

The takeaway is simple. Athletes, coaches, and fitness fans should be strategic, not habitual, with ice baths.

“Cold-water immersion is not a one-size-fits-all recovery tool,” remarked lead author Erfan Berjisian, a PhD student at ECU.

“Its benefits depend heavily on the athlete’s goals, the type of exercise completed, and when the next performance session is scheduled.”.

The review found ice baths are particularly good at reducing muscle soreness. They also lower markers of muscle damage and they help athletes feel recovered faster.

According to recent reports, muscle soreness dropped consistently for up to four days after exercise. Markers of muscle damage were lower between 24 and 72 hours after an ice bath.

The review also noted a boost in heart rate variability right after exercise. That’s a sign the body is starting to recover.

For athletes who need to compete again soon, the benefits depend on what they’ll be doing and how much time they have to recover.

“Cold-water immersion appears especially useful when recovery time is limited, such as during tournaments, congested competition schedules or repeated high-intensity training sessions,” Berjisian said.

Sources indicate that researchers found endurance performance improved within the first hour after an ice bath. Power and jump performance often improved 24 to 72 hours later.

However, explosive performance actually dropped in the hours right after an ice bath.

That likely happens due to the temporary cooling effect on muscles.

“If athletes need to perform high-speed or explosive movements soon after cooling, cold-water immersion may be counterproductive unless sufficient re-warming occurs,” stated co-author Kristina Kendall from ECU.

Perhaps the most significant finding was about repeated use.

Athletes who constantly used cold-water immersion after resistance training saw smaller improvements in strength, muscle size, and power.

The evidence suggests chronic use may blunt some of the body’s normal muscle-building responses to training.

Sources indicate that the review also found a detail worth noting. The effect on strength may depend on the protocol.

Recent findings suggest that immersing just the exercised limb was linked to reduced gains. Whole-body immersion highlighted no clear detrimental effect.

According to recent reports, for endurance athletes, it  was a different story. The review found no evidence that regular cold-water immersion harmed aerobic fitness or endurance adaptations.

The results suggest that cold-water immersion at 50–59°F (10–15°C) for 10–15 minutes generally helped with post-workout recovery.

Colder water, at 41–50°F (5–10°C) for the same duration, may help restore jumping performance and lower markers of muscle damage.

Both intermittent and continuous protocols worked, with no clear winner between them.

The authors also assessed the quality of that evidence. They rated it low to very low.

Most of the samples were male, which limits how well the findings apply to women.

In a recent development, the authors also flagged some overlap between the reviews, especially the ones on strength and muscle growth. Those conclusions rest on a fairly concentrated group of trials.

The review calls for more work on women and on different training types. It also wants research that tracks athletes over longer periods.

Ice baths may ease soreness when athletes have limited time to recover, and their effects on performance vary with the activity and the timing.

But the science notes athletes should stop treating them as a cure-all.

They should be more cautious when the goal is building strength and muscle mass.

In a recent development, when races or matches are only a day or two apart, an ice bath may ease soreness before the next event. That can matter during a tournament, when athletes have little time to recover between rounds.

If your goal is to build muscle or get stronger, consider saving the cold plunge for competition days.

Making it a routine after lifting may limit the gains you’re training for.

The study is published in the journal Sports Medicine – Open.

Male bumblebees usually leave the nest, so what happens when they stay?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lab experiments found that male bumblebees use their body heat to warm developing young, a task usually associated with queens and workers.
  • In a bumblebee nest, nearly all of the work has long been credited to the females.
  • In a recent development, the queen founds the colony and her daughters raise the young.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lab experiments found that male bumblebees use their body heat to warm developing young, a task usually associated with queens and workers.

In a bumblebee nest, nearly all of the work has long been credited to the females.

In a recent development, the queen founds the colony and her daughters raise the young. Males are expected to leave soon after reaching adulthood, mate and then die.

A latest study of lab-reared common eastern bumblebees has now found males helping with the young. The developing brood was warmed by the males with their own body heat.

Queens housed with males laid eggs sooner. After 28 days, nests with five males contained about 49 eggs, larvae and pupae on average, compared with 33 in nests with a queen alone.

Recent findings suggest that the experiments were run by Meghan Moore and Hollis Woodard at the University of California, Riverside. Both are entomologists. Their nests were not natural ones.

Queens were housed with as many as five males and no workers, a mix rarely seen in the wild.

Sources indicate that the project began with photos taken for a different experiment. Moore had pointed a thermal camera at the nests. Bright white patches of heat demonstrated up on the males.

Bumblebees raise their eggs, larvae and pupae together in a single clump. Biologists call these young the brood. A queen keeps the brood warm much as a hen warms her eggs.

Recent findings suggest that she straddles the clump and presses her abdomen against it. The heat is produced by muscles in her thorax, the middle part of her body.

This posture was first described in 1972 for another bumblebee species.

On each of 12 days, every nest was photographed four times within one hour. In total, 2,304 usable thermal images were collected.

The images were labeled so that scorers could not tell which kind of nest each one showed.

Males in the queen’s posture turned out to be hot. Their thoraxes averaged 94.6°F (34.8°C). Males standing on the brood without that posture averaged about 88°F (31°C).

Industry observers note that queens in the same posture averaged about 99°F (37.2°C). The males were not simply resting on a warm spot. Heat was being made in their bodies the way a queen makes it, only less of it.

Heat generated in the thorax is passed back to the abdomen. That rear section is the part a bee presses against the brood. Here, too, queens and males behaved differently.

According to recent reports, in incubating queens, the abdomen was about 2.9°F (1.6°C) cooler than the thorax. In incubating males, the abdomen was 6.7°F (3.7°C) cooler. Their gap was more than twice as wide.

Sources indicate that A possible reason was offered by the authors, who described it as speculation. Heat is known to damage sperm, including in males of another bumblebee species.

By limiting the heat that reaches his abdomen, a male may protect his sperm.

No sperm were examined in this study. For now the idea remains untested.

Moore and Woodard began the nest experiment with 75 mated queens. Each queen had been treated with carbon dioxide. This let her skip winter dormancy and begin laying eggs.

Some queens were given a nest box to themselves. Others shared a box with one, three or five young males from other colonies.

Queens living alone needed about 15 days to lay their first eggs. With one male, the wait dropped to about 11 days. It fell to about eight days with three males and about six with five.

A queen with five males therefore started laying in less than half the time of a lone queen.

Sources indicate that every nest was then allowed 28 days to grow, counted from its first eggs. An earlier start on egg laying could not explain a bigger nest at the end.

Fifteen queens died before the experiment was over. The brood counts come from the nests that remained.

After those 28 days, nests of lone queens held about 33 eggs, larvae and pupae on average.

Nests with five males held about 49. That is roughly 1.5 times as many. Nests with one or three males fell in between.

Industry observers note that only the nests with five males produced more adult workers during that time. They averaged about five workers per nest. The other groups averaged two or three.

Queens were photographed incubating about as often whether or not males were present.

The photos also revealed fewer instances in which no bee was incubating the brood when males were present.

Incubation helps maintain nest temperatures, which in turn support the brood’s development. Where males were photographed incubating more often, more older brood was found at the end.

According to the authors, male incubation may directly support the growth of the brood. They also wrote that more work is needed to show cause.

Sources indicate that nests holding males but no workers are unusual. For that reason a smaller test was also run. Five nests containing both males and worker bees were filmed for 24 hours in darkness with infrared cameras.

Males incubated in all five nests. Two of the nests were young, with fewer than 15 bees. Two others were mature, with 50 or more.

On video, a male can be picked out by a patch of facial hair. It is sometimes described as a moustache.

Male incubation is not a upcoming observation.

It has been revealed that in 1985, entomologist Sydney Cameron reported that males of a different bumblebee species incubate pupae. Moore and Woodard have now added a second species.

They also measured how nests developed when males were present.

In a recent development, how often males do any of this in wild nests cannot yet be noted. Young wild nests usually hold a queen and her workers. Males mostly appear late in the season.

Sources indicate that the lab males were also unable to leave. Any male inclined to fly off had no way to do so. The authors wrote that this may have made the males more likely to incubate.

Recent findings suggest that the bees came from commercially reared colonies, which may behave differently from wild ones. They were also given food instead of foraging for it.

Wild bumblebee nests are hard to find. As a result, data on wild colonies that produce males early are scarce.

Incubation takes a great deal of energy. What that work costs a male, in energy or in fertility, was not measured.

“What’s the trade-off? There’s no free lunch,” Woodard remarked.

According to recent reports, further studies are planned on whether caring for brood affects the males’ bodies. Future research will also need to test whether male incubation itself makes nests grow. Its importance in wild colonies is still unknown.

The full study was published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews
