#54333. What can AI learn from a thousand days of hearing what a baby hears?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1285 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

What can AI learn from a thousand days of hearing what a baby hears?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1285 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Princeton recorded eight babies for their first 1,000 days, and a model trained on one child's audio learned language on the same schedule.
  • A toddler can pick up hundreds of words just by hearing people talk.
  • Researchers at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute wired up 15 homes with cameras and microphones and recorded babies for most of their waking hours across the first 1,000 days of life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Princeton recorded eight babies for their first 1,000 days, and a model trained on one child's audio learned language on the same schedule.

A toddler can pick up hundreds of words just by hearing people talk. Could a computer start from scratch and recognize many of those same words on roughly the same timetable?

Researchers at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute wired up 15 homes with cameras and microphones and recorded babies for most of their waking hours across the first 1,000 days of life.

The researchers turned speech recorded around eight children into clean audio using synthetic voices.

They trained a separate model on each child’s audio in the order the speech was originally recorded.

The models identified recurring sound patterns that corresponded to words.

On average, each model reached the halfway point on a vocabulary checklist within 22 days of the child it was paired with.

“We wanted to turn the usual logic of developmental research around,” mentioned Uri Hasson, a professor of psychology and neuroscience at Princeton who led the study.

“Instead of observing a child for an hour in the laboratory, we asked whether we could build a model capable of learning and immerse it in the child’s actual experience, day after day.”.

The families were in New Jersey and spanned a range of incomes and backgrounds. Each home got four to 14 recording devices spread across two to five rooms.

The devices ran 12 to 14 hours a day, from February 2022 to May 2025.

In a recent development, the project gathered roughly 1.2 million hours of audio and video, of which the eight homes analyzed in this paper supplied about 600,000. An automated pipeline worked out where the child was in the house and pulled out the speech happening nearby.

Recent findings suggest that each child ended up with between 1,900 and 6,600 hours of usable speech, three to seven and a half hours a day. That adds up to 6 to 27 million words per child, over a median of 960 recording days.

Every month from eight months on, caregivers filled out a standard checklist of which words their child understood and stated. Those forms are how the researchers knew what each child knew, and when.

Industry observers note that children reached half of the 649-word checklist anywhere from about 12 to 22 months old. That ten-month spread between children is the thing most studies average away.

Recent findings suggest that the model started from random numbers. It had no dictionary, no phonetics, no notion of where one word ends and the next begins, and no text.

Recent findings suggest that the program’s first part chops the incoming sound into 20-millisecond pieces and sorts them into categories it invents for itself. Its second part tries to guess the next piece from what came before.

Whenever a run of pieces becomes reliably predictable, the program files it away as a unit, which is the closest thing it has to a word.

According to recent reports, nothing about that design is specific to English or even to speech. What makes it unusual is the schedule.

The audio arrives in the order it was recorded, one day at a time, rather than shuffled into batches the way an AI language model is normally trained.

At the end of each simulated day, the program gets a sample of speech from earlier days, weighted toward recent ones. The researchers call it replay.

According to recent reports, english has 39 phonemes, the sound units that distinguish bat from pat. Children spend their first year tuning in to the ones their own language uses.

Within roughly 12 to 15 months of simulated time, the program had carved out dedicated categories for nearly all of them.

Across the eight children, the models averaged 37.5 phonemes each. The lowest count came from the household with the least recording.

The order it happened in, sounds before words, is the order infants follow.

Sources indicate that words came after. For the child the paper calls Coral, the checklist noted she understood 97 words at 12 months, and her model had 91.

Across all eight children, the models and the children hit the same vocabulary milestones within an average of 22 days of each other, with the worst case 56 days.

The models also reproduced the differences between children, landing close to each child’s own halfway age.

They did not match perfectly. The models tended to start learning words a little late and then catch up faster, so the shape of the curve was only partly right.

The surprise in the paper is what happened when the researchers took replay away.

Coral’s household produced something like 10 million words a year, which is a rich environment by any measure. Hearing all of it once, in order, wasn’t enough. With a single pass the program barely learned words at all.

Around 25 to 30 passes over each day’s material was enough, and more than that added very little.

Industry observers note that the researchers link this to what sleep is thought to do for memory. A program replaying audio files is not a sleeping infant, and the paper is careful about that.

Industry observers note that the amount of recording mattered just as much. Fed only a tenth of Coral’s daily speech, under an hour a day, the program learned none of the checklist words by 24 months.

At 30% of the day, about two and a half hours, it learned 80 of the 649 checklist words.

At 70% it got about nine-tenths of the way to the full result. The rarer words, it seems, only turn up for a listener who is there most of the day.

One limitation shapes everything else. Household recordings are full of clattering dishes, television, and two people talking at once, and the program was not asked to cope with any of that.

Instead the researchers transcribed all the speech around each child, then had a text-to-speech system read the transcripts back as clean audio.

Each household got a mix of eight adult female voices, with 30% of segments read in a voice matched to the child’s mother.

Sources indicate that so the word order, the timing and the vocabulary are real, and the sound isn’t. The acoustic problem a baby actually solves, picking one voice out of a noisy room, was left for later work.

Three of the eight children also had shorter recordings, 14 to 20 months of usable input, so their later trajectories are extrapolated rather than modeled.

The program also sees nothing: no faces, no pointing, no object being handed over, which is a large part of how toddlers work out what a word refers to.

According to recent reports, the program learned sounds and words. It did not learn grammar, and whether the same machinery would arrive at sentence structure is the open question the authors name.

The team wants to use the setup for questions nobody can put to a real baby. What would less sleep do, or screen speech instead of a parent’s?

Future studies could also add eye contact and the rest of the social world the cameras captured but the model never saw.

Hadas Raviv, a computational cognitive scientist in Princeton’s psychology department who built the analysis pipeline, framed the goal as the opposite of the usual one in artificial intelligence.

“Unlike much of modern AI, which aims for superhuman performance, we’re trying to understand how humans learn and how that learning gives rise to intelligence,” Raviv remarked.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

  • A six-week trial found that inulin fiber supplements modestly reduced knee osteoarthritis pain and improved grip strength in some adults.
  • Adults with knee osteoarthritis who took inulin, a fiber found in chicory root, ended a six-week trial with less knee pain than volunteers on a placebo.
  • Industry observers note that volunteers who took inulin alone also gained grip strength, a moderate effect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A six-week trial found that inulin fiber supplements modestly reduced knee osteoarthritis pain and improved grip strength in some adults.

Adults with knee osteoarthritis who took inulin, a fiber found in chicory root, ended a six-week trial with less knee pain than volunteers on a placebo. On a scale from zero to ten, their scores fell 1.11 points more.

Industry observers note that volunteers who took inulin alone also gained grip strength, a moderate effect. Those who followed a digital exercise program, or combined both treatments, did not.

The work was led by the University of Nottingham in England, and its results appeared in February 2026.

Recent findings suggest that in 2019, about 528 million people worldwide were living with osteoarthritis, according to the World Health Organization. The knee is the joint most often affected, with 365 million cases.

Recent findings suggest that about 33 million U.S. adults have the condition, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates. Physical exercise may help relieve pain and improve function, the agency notes.

In the U.K., 5.4 million people have knee osteoarthritis, according to a 2025 report from the charity Arthritis UK.

“Our recent lived experience survey demonstrated that six in ten people are living in pain most or all of the time due to their arthritis,” noted Professor Lucy Donaldson, the charity’s director of research.

Under its former name, Versus Arthritis, the charity was one of the trial’s funders.

Between May 2022 and February 2025, the researchers randomly assigned 136 adults to four groups, and 117 completed all assessments.

Those who finished averaged 67.5 years of age, and 58.1 percent were women.

One group took 0.7 ounces (20 grams) of inulin powder a day. A second followed Joint Academy, a digital physical therapy program that began with a call to a personal physical therapist.

Recent findings suggest that A third group combined both, and a fourth took maltodextrin, a starch-based powder, as a placebo. For ethical reasons linked to blood sugar, the placebo dose was half the inulin dose.

In a recent development, volunteers did not know whether they were taking inulin or the placebo, but those assigned to exercise knew it. The staff who measured outcomes were blinded to all treatments.

Inulin’s pain result only just reached statistical significance, with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning 0.04 to 2.18 points.

Exercise lowered pain scores by 1.55 points compared with placebo, and the combination by 1.67 points. No added benefit from combining the two emerged, though the sample was too small to reliably detect one.

According to recent reports, on average, both single treatments exceeded the one-point drop that patients typically notice as meaningful. Exercise came close to the two-point threshold for feeling “much better.”.

A third of placebo takers also improved by at least one point, but only 11 percent improved by two points or more.

Inulin made people less sensitive to pressure and to repeated painful stimuli, two measures linked to how the nervous system processes pain. Exercise alone had no such effect.

Sources indicate that “This study raises the exciting possibility that a simple dietary change – adding a fibre supplement to your breakfast or yogurt – could meaningfully reduce pain and improve physical function,” said Dr. Afroditi Kouraki of the University of Nottingham’s School of Medicine, the lead author.

Recent findings suggest that exercise improved a timed up-and-go test and a 30-second chair-stand test. Inulin alone had no effect on either.

Inulin feeds gut bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids. Only inulin raised blood levels of butyrate, one of those fatty acids, and of GLP-1, a hormone made in the gut.

Within the inulin groups, higher GLP-1 was associated with better grip strength, in an exploratory analysis that needs independent replication. The authors offer no explanation for the combined group’s grip result.

“The link we observed between GLP-1 and grip strength is particularly intriguing and points to a broader gut-muscle-pain axis that warrants further investigation,” said Professor Ana Valdes, the senior author, also of the School of Medicine.

According to recent reports, A 2024 Canadian trial of a similar fiber in adults with knee osteoarthritis and obesity reported gains in grip strength and mobility after six months. Its effect on knee pain was only a trend.

The short duration may not capture the full effects of exercise, the researchers acknowledged. Expectation effects in the exercise groups cannot be ruled out either.

It has been revealed that dropout reached 21 percent in the two exercise groups, compared with 3.6 percent in the two groups without exercise. To compensate, allocation odds were shifted toward exercise during later recruitment, which may have introduced bias.

A second analysis that included dropouts, with missing scores statistically imputed, gave consistent results. Only the effect of exercise on the up-and-go test lost statistical significance.

Of 50 inulin takers who finished, 23 reported minor digestive effects such as wind and bloating. None stopped the supplement or dropped out because of them.

In a recent development, U.K. government guidelines cited by the National Health Service call for 1.1 ounces (30 grams) of fiber a day, so the inulin dose alone supplied two-thirds of that.

Valdes sits on the scientific advisory boards of the nutrition organization Chuckling Goat and of OLIPOP, roles declared unrelated to this study.

The study was published in the journal Nutrients.

Sources indicate that compared to window or portable air conditioners, ductless systems are more permanent, more powerful, and typically quieter. They also give you more control over specific rooms, so you can cool the spaces you actually use instead of the whole house at once. There are some drawbacks, though.

Ductless ACs run pricey (even setting aside the cost of installation). They’re also more visible than central air vents, and you need to size and place them carefully to cool a room evenly. DIY installs or wrong-sized units can cause complications in the long run.

In a recent development, maintenance can also be difficult, as not all HVAC professionals are familiar with these products. However, for an older home with radiator heat (like mine is), it’s the best way to add efficient air conditioning without blocking most of our windows.

First, decide how many indoor units you need and where you’ll place them. Unlike window units, mini-split systems are permanent fixtures, so carefully consider where they’ll be most efficient within your home.

Industry observers note that generally, a single ductless air conditioner can handle cooling a targeted area or a single room. If you’re cooling down multiple rooms, consider a multi-zone system so that you get even temperatures throughout your home.

It’s also essential to select a unit that’s powerful enough for the room it’s in—too small and it may not cool your space. The cooling capacity of air conditioners is typically measured in British Thermal Units, or BTUs, per hour.

Recent findings suggest that as a general rule of thumb, choose a unit that delivers 20 BTUs per square foot of living space. So, a 200-square-foot room needs at least a 4,000-BTU air conditioner. Those sensitive to noise should consider units with a quiet mode feature.

Quieter units are more desirable for bedrooms, living rooms, and nurseries, where a peaceful environment is essential. Look for ductless air conditioners with noise levels between 19 and 30 decibels, since this range can be compared to the sound of leaves rustling or a soft whisper.

Units with levels between 30 to 40 decibels are still suitable for other areas of the home, since this range is comparable to background noise or casual conversation.

Recent findings suggest that while shopping for your ductless air conditioner, you may see “SEER” with a number next to it. SEER stands for Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio, which measures how much energy your air conditioner uses during the annual cooling season. The higher the SEER rating, the less energy your unit uses to cool your home.

You may also see “SEER2,” a newer efficiency standard introduced in 2023 that uses updated testing conditions meant to better reflect real-world performance. SEER2 numbers are typically slightly lower than SEER ratings for the same unit, but they represent the same idea: higher numbers mean more efficient energy usage.

In a recent development, A product with an Energy Star certification has been rigorously tested by the United States Environmental Protection Agency for its energy efficiency. EPA-recognized laboratories test products to Energy Star specifications to ensure manufacturers produce energy-saving products.

Although testing guidelines change per product category, all items must prove they consume less energy than standard models without compromising performance.

Mini-splits are more permanent and expensive than window or portable air conditioners, so they make the most sense when you plan to cool the same space for several seasons. Most systems also require professional installation, and larger units may need electrical upgrades before you can install them.

Sources indicate that they’re also not invisible. The indoor air handler usually stays mounted high on the wall year-round, which may bother homeowners who prefer the low-profile look of central air vents. Proper sizing and placement matter, too, since an oversized, undersized, or poorly positioned unit can lead to uneven cooling, wasted energy, or poor humidity control.

Sources indicate that ductless air conditioners cool your home without using the network of ducts that central HVAC systems rely on, notes Lincoln. “The way I explain ductless cooling to homeowners is simple: the system conditions the room directly instead of trying to send cooled air through ductwork first,” she explains.

Instead, ductless air conditioners connect a small outdoor condenser to one or more indoor air handlers using refrigerant lines. Because there’s no ductwork involved, these types of units are often more efficient and easier to install in older homes, additions, or finished spaces where running ducts would be difficult. They also allow for “zoned” cooling, meaning you can control the temperature in individual rooms instead of conditioning the entire house at once.

Sources indicate that these systems are also more customizable than a whole-house system. “Where mini-splits really shine is zoning,” explains Lincoln. “One outdoor unit can support multiple indoor heads, so different parts of the house can be conditioned based on how those spaces are actually used.”.

Yes. “A mini-split is just a ductless system made up of an outdoor condenser and one or more indoor air handlers,” notes Lincoln. The terms ductless air conditioner and mini-split are generally used interchangeably, as we have in this guide.

Sources indicate that both describe systems that pair an outdoor condenser with one or more indoor air handlers connected by refrigerant lines instead of ductwork. The “split” part refers to the system being divided between indoor and outdoor components.

Some mini-splits provide cooling only, but many modern models are actually heat pumps, meaning they can both cool and heat your home using the same system. Adding air conditioning to an older home that previously utilized radiator or baseboard heat can be tricky—squeezing ductwork into closets and unused corners feels a bit like remodelling Jenga. These units solve that matter without much fuss.

Usually, yes. In most cases, it makes sense to hire a professional. Installing a mini-split usually involves mounting indoor and outdoor units, running refrigerant lines, and making electrical connections, which is why many manufacturers recommend professional installation.

Recent findings suggest that “Installation is where good equipment gets made—or wasted,” advises Lincoln. “Mini-splits look deceptively simple once they’re on the wall, but installation is not casual work. Line sets, electrical, drainage, vacuuming the system down properly before startup…those are the steps that determine whether the unit runs the way it was engineered to run.”.

Some systems are more DIY-friendly, but even those can be complicated if you’re not comfortable working with electrical systems or HVAC equipment. Professional installation also helps ensure the system runs efficiently and may be required to maintain the manufacturer’s warranty. If you are a very seasoned DIY pro who’s handy with a YouTube tutorial, you might be okay. Otherwise, we recommend budgeting for an installer.

Companies size mini-splits systems based on BTUs, which measure how much heating or cooling power the unit can deliver.

It has been revealed that “When people ask how to calculate the right BTU for a room, the honest answer is that manufacturer charts are a starting point, not a finish line,” says Lincoln. “For a window unit, those charts can get you close. For a mini-split, a proper load calculation is the better answer.” This is another reason it’s great to work with an expert installer before ordering—they can guide your purchasing based on your needs.

Recent findings suggest that lincoln explains that it’s not a straightforward calculation, in most cases. “Room size is only the starting point. Sun exposure, ceiling height, insulation, window size, window direction, occupancy, and heat from electronics or appliances all change the cooling load,” she adds.

Smaller systems around 9,000 BTU often work for bedrooms or small offices, while 12,000–18,000-BTU systems handle larger living areas. As a rough rule, most homeowners look at units sized for the square footage of the space they want to heat or cool, but must consider all of these other factors, too.

#54330. The next ice age may have begun 2,000 years ago, but humans cut it short

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1241 w)

The next ice age may have begun 2,000 years ago, but humans cut it short

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1241 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buried plants on Baffin Island reveal when a remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet began growing again and how human-caused warming reversed its advance.
  • About 2,000 years ago, the last remnant of the ice sheet that once covered much of Canada began growing again on Baffin Island.
  • It expanded in bursts, then began retreating around 1960 as warmer summers melted more ice than winters added.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buried plants on Baffin Island reveal when a remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet began growing again and how human-caused warming reversed its advance.

About 2,000 years ago, the last remnant of the ice sheet that once covered much of Canada began growing again on Baffin Island.

It expanded in bursts, then began retreating around 1960 as warmer summers melted more ice than winters added.

The researchers argue that the regrowth marked the earliest stage of a new glaciation in North America, and that human-caused warming cut it short.

At the peak of the last glacial period, the Laurentide Ice Sheet covered much of Canada and reached into the northern United States.

“People always say that it disappeared, but that’s not true,” stated Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory who led the study.

Sources indicate that what’s left of it is the Barnes Ice Cap, on the central plateau of Baffin Island in Nunavut. Its bedrock is low for the Canadian Arctic, only about 1,640 feet (500 meters) above sea level.

The ice has lasted this long because it is roughly 2,300 feet (700 meters) thick, enough to lift its surface to where snow survives the summer.

Sources indicate that young’s team wanted to know whether the ice cap had ever been smaller than it is today and then grown back. Gifford Miller of the University of Colorado Boulder was among the co-authors.

The answer matters beyond one ice cap, because models say glaciations over North America most likely begin on Baffin Island.

Sources indicate that the Barnes Ice Cap is frozen to the rock beneath it, so it doesn’t slide the way most glaciers do. Instead of grinding the ground as it spreads, it buries whatever is growing there and preserves it.

When the margin retreats, the moss and small plants it killed centuries ago come out of the ice.

Radiocarbon dating estimates when the plants died, giving researchers a way to date the ice’s advance.

Young’s team collected 88 of those plants at or near the 2022 ice edge. About 70% of them died around the year 1800, give or take 200 years. Those were the coldest summers of the Little Ice Age.

According to recent reports, sixteen more came from a half-mile (800-meter) line running out from the ice edge. A drained lake there had let the margin retreat farther than anywhere else.

In an interview with Earth.com, Young said that result surprised the team.

The researchers hadn’t expected the ice cap to have been smaller than it is now at any point in the last several thousand years.

“This unique finding allowed us to unexpectedly use these plants to track the ice cap’s renewed expansion,” Young noted.

The researchers also dated 35 boulders and bedrock surfaces around the ice cap. Rock that is open to the sky builds up a rare form of beryllium at a known rate.

The amount in a surface tells how long it has been uncovered.

All of the surfaces gave the same answer: the old ice sheet had retreated inside its 2022 position about 3,600 years ago.

The oldest plants along the half-mile line died around the year 1000, so the ice was already advancing by then.

Industry observers note that to fill the gap, the team turned to 186 radiocarbon dates from plants under smaller ice caps on the same plateau. Not one of those dates is older than the Common Era.

The authors read that as the moment, roughly 2,000 years ago, when the summer snowline dropped onto the plateau and ice began to build up across it.

So the Laurentide reached its smallest size between about 3,000 and 2,000 years ago and then started to grow. The authors count that reversal as the start of the next glaciation.

The ice advanced in pulses during cold spells and was nearing its largest modern extent by about 1800.

By 1960 the growth had stopped. Aerial photographs show the margin retreating from about 1961, and the ice cap has since given up between 650 and 2,600 feet (200 and 800 meters) of ground.

Snow also survives the summer on less and less of it.

According to recent reports, around 1960, about 35% of its surface was high enough for snow to last through the summer. By the early 2000s only 3% was, and since 2010 none of it has been.

There is no longer any part of the ice cap where snow can pile up and turn into ice.

In a recent development, summer temperatures have been climbing since the late 1700s, and since the early 1960s warmer summers account for almost all of the ice cap’s losses. Those summers track the greenhouse gases people have added to the air.

According to recent reports, between 1750 and 1850, the total rose by only about 12 parts per million of carbon dioxide equivalent. By 1960 it had risen another 50, and by 2024 another 138.

“The expansion and retreat of ice sheets has been one of Earth’s most consistent patterns over the last 2.6 million years,” Young told Earth.com.

About 2,000 years ago, he said, the Laurentide was starting its next phase of expansion, as it should have. Then greenhouse gases ended that expansion in the middle of the 20th century.

In the 1970s, some climate scientists argued that a new ice age was coming, and the idea got a famous airing in Newsweek.

Industry observers note that young stated those scientists were essentially correct, even if the media twisted the story. “We did just barely start the next glaciation, but they didn’t know it at the time,” he said.

Behind that growth was a slow decline in summer sunlight at high northern latitudes, the orbital rhythm that paces ice ages.

Industry observers note that greenhouse gases did rise over those thousands of years, by about 20 parts per million. The authors found that was too small to overcome the cooling.

Recent findings suggest that computer models suggest the next glaciation will not begin for thousands of years. But those models usually define its start as the point where fresh ice sheets hold enough ice to lower the sea by about 10 feet (3 meters) or more.

Young’s team said that would miss the earlier stage of ice growth that his team considers the start of a glaciation.

In a recent development, A 2025 study built from ocean sediments and Earth’s orbit estimated that the first regrowth of ice in this interglacial would come somewhere in the last 1,800 years or so. The plants on Baffin Island agree.

In a recent development, what the record can’t yet say is exactly when the regrowth began. The plants that would date it are still under the ice, and only continued retreat will bring them out.

The dates so far are archived at the NSF Arctic Data Center.

Young said models of the ice cap’s future have it disappearing completely within the next few hundred years.

Asked what happens once the last piece of the Laurentide is gone, Young said another glaciation is unlikely anytime soon.

“Given the amount of greenhouse gases that are in the atmosphere and that we continue to pump, the next glaciation is a long way off,” he remarked.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

  • They took them to the San Francisco Zoo, where the snakes gave birth later that year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

62 endangered San Francisco garter snakes born at the San Francisco Zoo were released in San Mateo County this fall, the first head-start release.

Sources indicate that in spring 2025, U.S. Geological Survey biologists caught 11 pregnant San Francisco garter snakes on the San Mateo County coast, in a preserve run by the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen).

They took them to the San Francisco Zoo, where the snakes gave birth later that year.

Sources indicate that after giving birth, the mothers were returned to the wild, the zoo says. The zoo’s team raised their young until they were massive enough to be released.

On November 10, 2026, the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens said 62 of those zoo-born garter snakes had been released this fall in San Mateo County.

It was the first release under a head-starting program for the endangered subspecies. The announcement does not say how many are still alive.

According to recent reports, the San Francisco garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia) is a subspecies of the common garter snake. The zoo says it lives only in San Mateo County and a small corner of Santa Cruz County.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service describes red on the top of the head, a greenish-blue or blue belly, a wide pale stripe down the back and red and black stripes on the sides.

It has been revealed that A major loss of habitat came after World War II. In the 1940s, the sag ponds along Skyline Boulevard, small ponds in low spots along a fault line, held hundreds of the snakes.

By the 1960s, nearly all of those ponds had been drained and built over, according to the Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy.

Industry observers note that the snake went onto the first federal endangered species list on March 11, 1967, six years before the Endangered Species Act of 1973. The zoo estimates that a couple thousand remain in the wild today.

Industry observers note that federal biologists blame illegal collection, construction, drought and saltwater in coastal ponds. Bullfrogs and largemouth bass are on the list too, because they eat the snakes and their prey.

That prey includes threatened California red-legged frogs, which the snakes rely on for food, the zoo says.

In a recent development, since 2004, the conservancy and the National Park Service have restored and enhanced 33 acres (13 hectares) of wetland, grassland and coastal scrub for the snakes, according to Midpen’s 2025 release. The work added upcoming ponds for breeding habitat.

In a recent development, garter snakes give birth to live young instead of laying eggs. In this subspecies, birth comes in July or August. A litter can hold 6 to 35 babies, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service species profile notes.

After the 11 females arrived, the team scanned them with ultrasound. The early scans showed that a goal of 80 to 120 live babies was feasible, Midpen reported in September 2025.

Later that month, the district estimated that the zoo’s Conservation Team was raising about 120 newborns.

The zoo had practice with the species. Its staff bred San Francisco garter snakes in the 1990s to work out how to keep them.

From 2005, they developed care protocols with the San Diego Zoo on housing, diet, growth tracking and parasite checks, Midpen noted in 2025.

Rochelle Stiles, the zoo’s director of field conservation, described the goal of the zoo’s snake rearing work.

“By providing these young snakes with a safe environment during their most vulnerable stage of life, we’re giving them a stronger start in the wild,” she stated.

Head-starting works that way. The young are fed and sheltered until they are massive enough to handle predators and competition for food, a method that also saved an endangered wallaby population in Australia.

Each snake born at the zoo had a genetic test before it left, and the results set its destination. About one-third went back to the area where its mother had been caught.

The rest went to several other populations that were short on both snakes and genetic variety. Isolated groups slowly lose diversity, the same problem behind a proposed genetic rescue for Lassen red foxes in northern California.

Recent findings suggest that disease data mattered too. Laura Patterson coordinates amphibian and reptile conservation statewide for the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW).

She noted a CDFW survey for snake fungal disease, an emerging disease found in many wild snakes, “aided in the selection process.”.

Recent findings suggest that the partners will not name the release sites. The zoo said secrecy protects the snakes from collectors, cars and disease.

Midpen biologist Karine Tokatlian also commented on the release. “Seeing these young snakes returning to the wild represents years of research, collaboration, habitat restoration and careful conservation work,” she mentioned.

In a recent development, removal from the endangered list requires at least 10 viable, self-sustaining breeding populations. Each one needs at least 200 snakes.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) ecologists had already tested the idea on a computer. In a 2023 paper in PLOS ONE, a team led by Jonathan Rose of the USGS Western Ecological Research Center simulated newly introduced populations started with newborns, juveniles, adults or a mix.

Head-started juveniles gave those populations the best chance of lasting. Releases would have to continue for at least 15 years to keep the risk of near-extinction low, the model noted.

Sources indicate that raising juveniles also takes fewer adults away from the donor site. Justin Sloan, acting deputy field supervisor at the USFWS Sacramento office, credited research, genetic testing, habitat work and specialized care.

Ariel Starr, a Midpen wildlife ecologist, looked beyond this one subspecies.

“The success of this project and the associated research will not only benefit the San Francisco garter snake but will also hopefully inform the recovery of many imperiled reptile species,” she said.

The November announcement gives no survival rate for the 62. It also does not say how long they had been out when it was posted.

Sources indicate that survival is low even for snakes born in the wild. One study found only 2 percent of females born live to age 5, according to the USFWS.

There is also a gap between the 2025 estimate of about 120 newborns and the 62 released. The zoo did not explain it.

The 2023 model focused on snake demography. Its authors wrote that the genetics of the donor, captive and released snakes would also be a major concern for any reintroduction blueprint.

Sources indicate that more than 130 garter snakes were born at the zoo in 2026. They are being raised for a second round of releases in 2027. Monitoring of both rounds will show whether the populations at the sites grow.

Rachel Townsend, a National Park Service wildlife biologist, put the first round in proportion. “Releasing these snakes is a significant moment, but it is one step of many in a much larger recovery effort,” she said.

It has been revealed that the mothers are back in the wild. This fall, 62 of their young were let go at sites the partners will not name.

The information was obtained from the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens.

A brain region known for listening helps us speak

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is important for talking, too.
  • Data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is important for talking, too.

Data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating. The results may help efforts to restore people’s voices. The results presented November 15 at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and published November 19 in Science.The study provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production, states neurologist and language researcher Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. “My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area” as an early stop on the pathway to saying a word.

A small part of the brain, just above the left ear, was first described in 1874 by a neurologist Carl Wernicke as necessary for making sense of speech. People with damage there had trouble comprehending words. But some people also had trouble producing them. “Sounds were swapped, words were replaced with near misses,” Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, said in a news briefing. “The basic question has been, ‘Why would damage to a hearing area of the brain break the ability to speak?’ That question has been open for 150 years.”The new research offers an answer: A small bit of Wernicke’s area (to be extremely specific, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus or lpSTG ) becomes active just before a word is spoken. “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it,” Chang said.

The finding adds to growing evidence that brain areas are more complex than people have appreciated, claims neuroscientist Leigh Hochberg at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “I believe that one of the things we are going to learn over the next five, 10 years of this research, is that each part of the brain that, we were taught as a med student or a grad student, does this, probably does that and a whole lot more.”.

Sources indicate that scientists measured brain activity in 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumors. They were able to see that this brain region kicked on as a person listened to words, and also just before they attempted to speak. Cells there had preferences for certain sorts of words, long ones, for instance. “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat,” said Matthew Leonard, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCSF.

It has been revealed that electrical stimulation to this small bit of brain also interfered with people’s ability to talk. “What we found was that stimulation, really only in this lpSTG area, disrupted this speech production when it was delivered just prior to speaking,” said UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva.

Some efforts to make implanted devices that can help restore speech to people who no longer talk focus on the motor cortex, a part of the brain that controls the movements required for speech. This bit of Wernicke’s area offers an additional spot to consider, Silva noted. “What if you could target a single brain region and gain access to the full spectrum of speech, from listening all the way up to speech production?”.

Experimental brain implants in two volunteers with paralysis were able to detect both what they heard and what they were trying to say, the researchers report in the study.

The discovery may help scientists better understand situations that involve both hearing and speaking, such as speech or comprehension differences in people with autism, or how children first begin learning to talk, Chang said.

Grand Canyon hotels reopen 81 days after a deadly flood, echoing a 1966 disaster

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Canyon's South Rim hotels reopen November 20 after an August flash flood cut off their water.
  • For the first time since the end of August, visitors can book a hotel room on the South Rim of the Grand Canyon again.
  • On Friday, November 20, the South Rim’s hotels reopened to overnight guests, including El Tovar, which has stood on the edge of the canyon since 1905.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Canyon's South Rim hotels reopen November 20 after an August flash flood cut off their water. In 1966, a flood wrecked 40% of the same pipeline project.

For the first time since the end of August, visitors can book a hotel room on the South Rim of the Grand Canyon again.

On Friday, November 20, the South Rim’s hotels reopened to overnight guests, including El Tovar, which has stood on the edge of the canyon since 1905.

They had been closed for 81 days. A flash flood on August 29 tore through Bright Angel Canyon, killed two hikers and badly damaged the pipeline that carries water to the South Rim.

It was not the first time. In 1966, while that same pipeline was being built, a flood destroyed or carried off about 40% of the project, according to the National Park Service.

The park confirmed on November 18 that six South Rim lodges would reopen on November 20: El Tovar Hotel, Thunderbird Lodge, Kachina Lodge, Bright Angel Lodge and Maswik Lodge, along with Yavapai Lodge, which is operated by Delaware North.

On the same day, the park moved from Stage 4 to Stage 3 water conservation measures, which it called an important milestone in the restoration of South Rim water services.

Food and drink services will resume gradually, and the park is asking visitors to check its website for dining hours.

It has been revealed that conserving water is still crucial. Guests, visitors and residents are asked to take shorter showers, turn off faucets when they are not in use and avoid unnecessary water use.

Recent findings suggest that the flash flood hit Bright Angel Canyon and the Phantom Ranch area at about 2:30 p.m. on August 29. By the next morning, 62 people had been evacuated from Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail.

Nearly all of the footbridges over Bright Angel Creek were destroyed.

Metal structures and debris washed into the Colorado River, which was closed to river traffic. In steep terrain, heavy rain can trigger flash floods in mountain rivers faster than expected.

Two hikers from Granbury, Texas, John Giusti, 46, and Brent Rosenkranz, 42, died in the flood.

A member of their hiking group was reported missing, and the park said in its September 8 update that one person remained unaccounted for.

The flood badly damaged the Transcanyon Waterline, a 12½-mile pipeline built in the 1960s.

It carries water from Roaring Springs, on the North Rim side, down through the canyon and up to the South Rim, where it supplies drinking water and fire protection for every facility, including more than 800 historic buildings.

The park’s drinking water comes from a single spring connected to more than 6 miles of caves.

About 40% of the old pipeline between the Phantom Ranch area and the North Rim was damaged, and the water intakes at Bright Angel Creek and Roaring Springs were hit hard.

On August 31, the park stopped all overnight stays at its hotels, including Phantom Ranch, and the South Rim began living on stored water.

It has been revealed that the park stayed open for day visits. When it unveiled the closure, it noted South Rim food and drink services, the Grand Canyon Clinic and the post office would remain open, some with reduced hours, while campers could only dry camp.

On September 16, a second flash flood damaged a temporary water intake that crews were building at Bright Angel Creek.

No one was hurt, but crews had to work out what repairs were needed and how the damage would affect the timeline.

On September 19, the park remarked it expected to start pumping water from the creek to a new treatment plant by November 16, and it was working on an agreement to haul about 200,000 gallons of water a day to keep its tanks from running low.

At the time, the South Rim was using about 137,000 gallons a day.

By November 18, the park mentioned water services to the South Rim were being restored, which allowed the hotels to reopen two days later.

The pipeline itself was born out of a water problem. From 1901 to 1932, the Santa Fe railroad brought drinking water to the South Rim by train every day, and the trains came back as needed until the late 1960s.

In the summer of 1961, a water train of 20 cars carried about 204,000 gallons.

According to recent reports, construction of the Transcanyon Waterline began in January 1965, using 6-inch and 8-inch aluminum pipe. Most of the equipment was designed specifically for the project, and the rest of the work was done by hand.

A year later, the project was nearly finished when what the park calls a 1,000-year flood struck.

Fifteen inches of rain fell on the inner canyon, and the water carried away trees, boulders and sections of new pipe.

A survey after the flood found that about 40% of the project was destroyed or missing. The cost rose from $2 million to $5 million, and construction resumed in late 1967.

The flood’s high-water mark is still recorded on the walls of the Phantom Ranch Ranger Station.

In a recent development, the old line was built to last about 30 years and has been in service for more than 50. Since 2010, it has suffered over 85 major breaks.

A single repair often costs more than $25,000, and crews can reach the inner canyon only by trail or helicopter.

Breaks had closed the hotels before. In December 2025, after three significant breaks since late October, the park suspended overnight stays on December 6 and reopened the lodges on December 17.

In 2023, the park began a $208 million project to replace the pipeline and modernize the water system.

The upcoming pipeline on the south side of the canyon was not damaged by either flood this year, and before August 29 the park was just over a month away from starting to use it.

Some inner canyon trails reopened in late October, including the South Kaibab Trail below the Tipoff and the River Trail.

But the Black Bridge, the Silver Bridge, Phantom Ranch and the entire North Kaibab Trail remained closed, and the park warned that water would stay off at Mile-and-a-Half and Three-Mile Resthouses and at Havasupai Gardens for the rest of the winter.

Hikers must carry all their water and a way to filter or treat it.

El Tovar, a National Historic Landmark since 1987, was built from local limestone and Oregon pine for nearly $250,000. The hotel, which has 78 rooms, is once again taking guests.

The park says water conservation remains vital as operations resume, and that the patience of residents, visitors and businesses during the emergency helped it keep essential services running.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s releases on the reopening of South Rim lodging, the August 29 flash flood, the recovery plan, the projected water dates, the August 31 hotel closure, the two hikers who died, the second flash flood, the trail reopenings and the December 2025 hotel reopening, its pages on the Transcanyon Waterline and its history, and its page on El Tovar Hotel.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

The red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

A newcomer to electoral politics, she rapidly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

According to recent reports, in 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

Running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch announced he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

Recent findings suggest that this year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1278 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Meerkats cross the desert together, but what happens when one finds itself alone?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers tracked 20 meerkats in the Kalahari Desert to see how they navigated familiar territory after being separated from their groups.
  • Meerkats leave their burrows together each morning and forage as a group.
  • In South Africa’s Kalahari Desert, researchers carried 20 adult meerkats up to 0.9 miles from where they caught them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers tracked 20 meerkats in the Kalahari Desert to see how they navigated familiar territory after being separated from their groups.

Meerkats leave their burrows together each morning and forage as a group. How well can one find its way alone?

In South Africa’s Kalahari Desert, researchers carried 20 adult meerkats up to 0.9 miles from where they caught them.

Industry observers note that after release, 18 reached a familiar spot or found their group. Fourteen headed first to the burrow where the group had slept.

The team found no clear advantage for older or more experienced animals.

The researchers suggest that daily group travel may give meerkats enough experience to navigate alone.

Sources indicate that the study was led by Mathilde Martin of the University of Zurich. The team worked alongside the Kalahari Meerkat Project, which follows about 15 wild groups accustomed to people.

The project is run from the Kalahari Research Centre, which is known as the KRC.

“At the KRC, our work with meerkats allows us to distract them with a water bottle and fit their collar in a few seconds while they stand upright drinking; a mere formality for them,” Martin said.

Industry observers note that A GPS tag on each collar logged the position of the animal once every second. A radio transmitter was also fitted, along with a small audio recorder for the meerkat’s calls.

The team tested a total of 20 adults from five groups between January and March 2025. Fifteen of these animals were male, whereas only five of them were female.

Each meerkat was caught while its group was foraging and was released up to 0.9 miles (1.5 kilometers) away.

Such a distance is greater than the ground usually covered by a meerkat group in a whole day.

The release sites were located inside the territory of each group. The team chose areas that the group had not visited for at least 30 days.

Homing experiments of this kind have previously been carried out on honeybees and desert ants. Highly social animals that travel in tight groups have rarely been tested in the same way.

This is because the knowledge of one animal is difficult to separate from the decisions of the group.

Industry observers note that eighteen of the 20 meerkats left the release site. The sleeping burrow, the capture spot or the group itself was reached by all 18 of them.

Some of the meerkats departed almost at once, whereas others circled the release site for nearly 90 minutes.

The area covered by them ranged from half an acre to almost 17 acres (2,050 to 68,200 square meters).

A meerkat rarely strayed from its course once a direction had been chosen. Sixteen of the animals aimed for a fixed place.

The sleeping burrow was visited first by 14 of those 16.

On average, the straight-line distance to the target amounted to 82% of the distance actually walked by the meerkat.

Industry observers note that the release areas had not been visited by the group for a month. The team therefore concluded that the meerkats had been navigating from long-term memory.

Sources indicate that two males never left the release site, and they were carried back to their groups after 90 minutes. They were no younger or less experienced than the others.

The authors suspect that stress kept them there, and not a lack of knowledge.

According to recent reports, some meerkats had been expected to navigate better than others. Subordinate males sometimes leave the group and go alone in search of mates.

Other females are occasionally driven out for a while by the dominant female.

Solo trips of this kind could be counted as practice. The researchers also considered the age of each animal, together with the time it spent on guard duty.

Attention was given as well to how often it scent-marked the territory or dug at shelters.

Sources indicate that none of those traits predicted how long a meerkat explored. Neither did they predict how accurately it set off or how straight it travelled.

No clear difference was found between males and females either, although only five females took part.

Industry observers note that the authors think that the explanation lies in the territory itself. It is small and stable, with 0.3 to 0.6 miles (0.5 to 1 kilometer) covered by a group daily.

The whole territory has probably been crossed several times by each member by the time adulthood is reached.

The authors wrote that pigeons of different ages are likewise able to find their way home equally well.

On the way home, the meerkats spent about two-thirds of their time searching for cues. Most of the remaining time was spent moving.

Few of them stopped to eat, and those that did only grabbed millipedes crawling on the sand.

The animals stood upright or climbed a bush or tree trunk in order to scan the landscape. Overall, they spent 10 times longer on looking than on sniffing.

It has been revealed that this balance between looking and sniffing was altered late in the trip. By that stage, a meerkat had reached its target and was searching for its group. Sniffing then took up more than 20% of its cue-searching time.

Recent findings suggest that along the way, meerkats were often seen sniffing around boltholes. These are the small shelters that the animals dig across their territory. An earlier experiment had found that meerkats remember where their boltholes are.

The authors suggested that boltholes may serve as landmarks in a meerkat’s memory of its territory.

The search was not ended by reaching the burrow, because the group could have moved on since the capture.

Thirteen of the 20 meerkats rejoined their groups on their own. The slowest took almost three hours.

The burrow or the capture site was reached by five others. The group had nevertheless not been found by them when the three-hour limit ran out.

These animals were caught again and returned by the team.

Sources indicate that the researchers could not explain why some meerkats succeeded while others did not. Success was not predicted by a straighter trip to the burrow.

Nor was it predicted by the number of scent marks left behind by the group.

According to recent reports, the tracking of a group was compared by the authors to a predator following its prey. The target keeps moving and its route is not known to the searcher.

Twenty animals make up a small sample, as the authors wrote. All of them were subordinate adults older than 10 months, so pups and dominant animals were not tested.

It has been revealed that every release was also made inside familiar territory. The results therefore do not show how a meerkat would manage in a place it does not know.

In a recent development, two reasons for looking around could not be fully separated either. A lone meerkat that scans the landscape may be checking for predators as much as searching for landmarks.

If many group members know the territory, the next question is who leads when the group moves.

The authors want to know whether certain traits influence which animal takes the lead. The physical needs of an animal and its social rank are two examples.

Co-author Benjamin Robira noted the team now wants to understand what makes up a meerkat’s mental picture of its territory.

The researchers also intend to study how the animals get from one point to another.

The full study was published in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

#54322. Rainforest ferns from an ancient lineage have a surprisingly young family tree

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (905 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Rainforest ferns from an ancient lineage have a surprisingly young family tree

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (905 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An ancient lineage of rainforest ferns reveals how rising mountains and retreating wetlands may have shaped plant diversity across tropical America.
  • In a recent development, some rainforest ferns belong to a lineage that stretches back to the age of dinosaurs.
  • Researchers at the University of Turku and Aarhus University have reconstructed the history of tropical American Danaea ferns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An ancient lineage of rainforest ferns reveals how rising mountains and retreating wetlands may have shaped plant diversity across tropical America.

In a recent development, some rainforest ferns belong to a lineage that stretches back to the age of dinosaurs. Yet roughly half its living species arose within the past six million years, as mountains rose and landscapes changed.

Researchers at the University of Turku and Aarhus University have reconstructed the history of tropical American Danaea ferns.

Industry observers note that the findings draw on decades of work identifying ferns and establishing where they grow. That groundwork made it possible to investigate how the group spread and diversified.

“We have conducted extensive research at the University of Turku in order to understand the biodiversity of the Amazon rainforest,” said senior author Hanna Tuomisto, a professor of ecology.

“In the last 25 years, we have discovered and described 47 new Danaea species previously unknown to science, and have clarified the distribution and phylogenetic relationships of the species in the Danaea genus.”.

“We have now been able to link this information to the geological and climatic history of tropical America.”.

The team combined DNA evidence from 78 species with 2,289 verified records of where the ferns grow. These records helped reconstruct where ancestral ferns probably lived and the elevations they occupied.

The genetic analysis included 11 species that had not yet been formally described.

The researchers’ preferred estimate suggests that the Danaea lineage split from the lineage of its closest living relatives about 128 million years ago, during the Early Cretaceous.

According to recent reports, the common ancestor of its surviving species lived much later, around 53 million years ago. The researchers traced that ancestor to Amazonia.

In a recent development, but an ancient lineage need not consist of ancient species. About half of today’s Danaea species originated during the past six million years.

This complicates a familiar explanation for tropical richness: favorable conditions allowed species to accumulate over immense stretches of time.

Persistence mattered, but the landscape also kept changing, creating opportunities for new species.

Fern diversity generally reaches its greatest heights in tropical mountain forests. Danaea follows a different pattern: Amazonia has consistently held its largest pool of species in the reconstruction.

It has been revealed that “Mountain rainforests are home in particular to an abundance of epiphytes – plants that grow on top of other plants. Danaea ferns, on the other hand, grow on the forest floor,” mentioned lead author Venni Keskiniva, a postdoctoral researcher at Turku.

“These research results are, in fact, similar to those obtained for trees, which are also the most species-rich in lowland rainforests.”.

Where a plant lives within a forest may therefore help explain where its group becomes most diverse. Findings from one fern group cannot automatically describe them all.

The Andes still played an key role. Although Amazonia contained more species, the mountains became the leading source of dispersal to other regions.

Sources indicate that mountain formation affected far more than the slopes themselves. As the Andes rose, they changed rainfall patterns along with the soils developing across neighboring lowlands.

Vast wetlands once occupied much of western Amazonia. Their drainage near the end of the Miocene opened additional land for forest plants to colonize.

The resulting western Amazonian soils were generally richer in nutrients and more variable, than soils in central Amazonia.

Those differences may have encouraged plants to specialize in different environments.

In a recent development, the timing fits the fern history. Most new Amazonian species arising within the past six million years appeared in western Amazonia during the last three million.

Newly introduced land in southern Central America also offered room for expansion. Arriving lineages frequently gave rise to additional species as the region’s landscapes developed.

The first mountain-adapted Danaea lineages appeared around 20 million years ago, following an intensification of Andean uplift. Several later spread into regions farther from the equator.

Their earlier move uphill may have helped them cope with the conditions they encountered there.

“As the plants had already adapted to the cooler climate of the mountains, it may have been easier for them to spread to areas where the temperature differences between the seasons are greater,” Keskiniva mentioned.

Lineages that remained adapted to Amazonian lowlands tended to stay within that region.

The repeated sequence of mountain colonization followed by expansion suggests that climate tolerance influenced which routes were available.

In a recent development, the mountains could both separate populations and help others reach latest habitats. Their role changed as the landscape rose and different fern lineages established themselves.

Sources indicate that assigning dates to this history was difficult. Many relevant fossils are fragmentary, and researchers disagree about where they belong in the family tree.

The team compared three dating approaches, which produced substantially different ages. It favored the reconstruction most consistent with other biological and geological evidence.

Industry observers note that the dates remain estimates, and coinciding events do not establish a cause by themselves. Still, the findings connect the survival of ancient lineages with much younger episodes of diversification.

“The biodiversity in rainforests is the result of a long history, but its formation has also been greatly influenced by events that are relatively recent on a geological time scale,” Keskiniva concluded.

The study is published in the journal Frontiers of Biogeography.

#54319. Nov. 19, 1969: Apollo 12 lands on the Moon

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (255 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Astronomy ↗ Open Full Page

Nov. 19, 1969: Apollo 12 lands on the Moon

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (255 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 14, 1969, launch amid stormy skies, Apollo 12’s Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed on the Moon in Oceanus Procellarum (the Ocean of Storms).
  • Although Bean accidentally pointed their color TV camera at the Sun, damaging it, both the Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) were otherwise successful.
  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

Five days after their Nov. 14, 1969, launch amid stormy skies, Apollo 12’s Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed on the Moon in Oceanus Procellarum (the Ocean of Storms). Part of Apollo 12’s mission was to demonstrate improvements to the precision of lunar landings, and Conrad piloted the Intrepid Lunar Module to a pinpoint landing on Nov. 19. While their crewmate Richard Gordon remained in the Command Module (Yankee Clipper) above them, Conrad and Bean began the first of their two moonwalks. Conrad descended the ladder from the LM first, and as he stepped onto the Moon quipped, “Whoopie! Man, that may have been a small one for Neil, but that’s a long one for me.”.

Although Bean accidentally pointed their color TV camera at the Sun, damaging it, both the Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) were otherwise successful. The astronauts collected rock and soil samples and deployed their Apollo Lunar Surface Experiment Package (ALSEP), which included a solar wind collector, and seismometer, and a magnetometer. They also visited the Surveyor 3 unmanned lander (which had been on the Moon since 1967), retrieving several components of the spacecraft to return to Earth for study. After 31 and a half hours on the Moon, nearly eight hours of those spent in EVAs, Intrepid lifted off and re-docked with Yankee Clipper. The crew safely splashed down back on Earth on Nov. 24.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#54318. Breaking: Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

Breaking: Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1486 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that early Wednesday (Nov.
  • The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.
  • In a recent development, the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a upcoming space exploration milestone: The probe, which rolled out in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.

The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.

In a recent development, the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe. But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us.

In a recent development, "What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker, who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong.".

Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaking discoveries, told through its incredible photos.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe rolls out atop a Titan/Centaur-6 launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Industry observers note that NASA's Voyager 2 probe launched before Voyager 1, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 took off a few weeks later, on Sept. 5. (The two spacecraft took slightly different routes through the solar system, allowing Voyager 1 to reach interstellar space first after a gravity boost from Jupiter and Saturn.).

Spilker, who joined NASA right out of college, attended the historic Voyager 2 launch and recalls "that feeling of watching the rocket lift up off the launchpad, feeling the roar of those rocket engines and knowing this was a mission going to visit places I'd always been curious about.".

A few weeks after launching, Voyager 1 took this photo of a crescent Earth and moon from 7.25 million miles (11.66 million km) from Earth.

On its way to the outer solar system, Voyager 1 snapped this image of a crescent Earth and its moon, captured in the same frame for the first time ever.

Sources indicate that voyager 1 photographed Jupiter from January to April 1979, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As the spacecraft zoomed closer to the giant planet, it snapped an image every 96 seconds, creating this incredible time-lapse animation of the planet's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of one Earth month.

Sources indicate that the close-up view showed that Jupiter is a far more dynamic world than previously thought. But Voyager also made key discoveries about the planet's many moons.

While passing by the Jovian moon Io, Voyager 1 witnessed an explosion: the first volcanic eruption ever seen beyond Earth. This proved that there were other geologically active worlds in our solar system, opening up entirely latest avenues of inquiry and exploration.

A blue eruption on Jupiter's moon Io, the first volcanic eruption seen on another world.

"Going in, we thought that the moons would look a lot like our own moon: ancient dead worlds," Spilker noted. "And yet we found out they were very different worlds — like Io with active volcanoes. It was just an incredible change in our thinking.".

Industry observers note that by viewing these eruptions, scientists saw parts of Io's surface being changed in real time. "As we got closer [to Io], scientists kept saying the surface is getting younger and younger, because they didn't see any massive craters, no medium sized craters, no little craters — until finally parts of its surface are just minutes old," Spilker remarked.

A mosaic view of Callisto taken from Voyager 1 photos at a distance of about 250,000 miles (400,000 km).

Some of Voyager's close-up observations also confirmed old theories. For example, Voyager 1's flyby of the moon Callisto in March 1979 revealed vast fields of well-preserved impact craters, proving that Callisto was geologically dead.

Jupiter and its thin ring of dust backlit by the sun in a Voyager 1 image.

In a recent development, A final surprise at Jupiter came when Voyager 1 swooped around the planet's nightside, seeing the gas giant backlit by the sun. This view revealed a thin ring system around the planet, made partly of the dust particles Io spewed into space.

Recent findings suggest that voyager 1 reached Saturn in November 1980 and made its closest approach to the planet on Nov. 12 of that year. Four days later, the spacecraft took this image of the planet's nightside, showing a broad shadow cast onto the surrounding rings.

"That is one of my favorite pictures: an outbound image, taken by Voyager looking at [Saturn] in a way you could never see from the Earth," Spilker remarked, noting that we can only ever see Saturn's sunlit side from our planet. "The rings just look so beautiful shining there, and you can actually see the shadow of Saturn on the rings themselves. It's a really, really special picture.".

In addition to discovering a previously unknown ring, Voyager 1 spotted five newly introduced moons around Saturn and took close-up photos of several other known satellites.

Voyager 1's closeup view of Titan revealed a dense, hazy atmosphere.

It has been revealed that the mission required Voyager to swing by the moon Titan in order to bend the probe's trajectory, sending it away from the solar system's planetary plane and toward a rendezvous with interstellar space. Before that, Voyager 1 revealed Titan's atmosphere to be so hazy that it completely obscured the moon's surface. This demonstrated that Titan's clogged atmosphere was far denser than those of Earth and Mars.

According to recent reports, by 1990, Voyager 1 was so far from the planetary plane that our solar system's planets looked like little more than specks of light. But before turning off its camera for good, Voyager 1 looked back at our cosmic neighborhood and took some of the most iconic space photos of all time.

Recent findings suggest that in a series of 64 images taken from roughly 40 times Earth's distance from the sun, Voyager snapped its solar system "family portrait," a mosaic of images capturing six planets together for the first time. The portrait included views of Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Frames from Voyager 1's family portrait showing Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The image of Earth from this collection is famously known as the "Pale Blue Dot.".

"We took the pictures of the planets in color, and that one is especially one of my favorites," Spilker said. "There's Earth captured in a sunbeam. A tiny world less than a pixel in size representing all the life that we know in our solar system — just a very special image reminding us just how special and precious our planet is.".

Earth appears as a pale blue dot in this iconic Voyager 1 image.

Recent findings suggest that voyager 1 turned off its camera immediately after taking these images, concluding its role as the greatest tourist in the history of our solar system. In 2012, Voyager 1 passed beyond the heliopause — the boundary where the sun's radiation gives way to the interstellar medium — becoming the first interstellar spacecraft in history.

Industry observers note that voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018 and is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035. In the meantime, several science instruments remain active on both probes, allowing them to measure the strange and mysterious environment between stars.

Even way out there, the probes are still detecting whispers of the sun's power.

Recent findings suggest that "We are still seeing effects from the sun that come out, hit the heliopause, and send shocks and pressure fronts out into the interstellar medium," Spilker said. "I wonder where we will finally reach the point where the sun doesn't influence what we're seeing, and we're in the pristine interstellar medium — and I hope that happens while Voyager 1 is still operating.".

He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.
