📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

Sources indicate that the animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, states Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

Industry observers note that the answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin says. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

Meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she states. But that’s not what the team discovered.

Industry observers note that in separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin claims.).

Neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin indicates. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

It’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she indicates, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every image of the cosmos is a translation of data.
  • Sources indicate that sonification does the same for the ears, turning an object’s brightness, color, and position into pitch, volume, and tone.
  • According to recent reports, our ears are acutely sensitive to shifts in pitch, and researchers in fields ranging from astronomy to volcanology have found that listening to data can reveal patterns a visual plot might hide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every image of the cosmos is a translation of data. The X-rays collected by NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory and the infrared light gathered by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) are invisible to our eyes, so astronomers assign them colors we can see. Even optical observations, from Hubble to backyard astrophotographers, translate, too, often assigning or enhancing color based on emission in various filters.

Sources indicate that sonification does the same for the ears, turning an object’s brightness, color, and position into pitch, volume, and tone. The idea dates back at least to the Geiger counter, invented in 1908, whose clicks intensify as radiation climbs. In 2020, the Chandra X-ray Center launched A Universe of Sound, NASA’s first ongoing program to sonify astronomical data.

According to recent reports, our ears are acutely sensitive to shifts in pitch, and researchers in fields ranging from astronomy to volcanology have found that listening to data can reveal patterns a visual plot might hide. Sonification also opens the cosmos to people who are blind or have low vision, for whom a processed image offers little.

RELATED: Listen to the universe: How sonification turns data into sound.

Recent findings suggest that on November 17, Chandra released four new sonifications, each built on a region where stars are forming right now. Young, massive stars blast out X-rays in fierce winds and outbursts, and studying those nurseries helps astronomers reconstruct how stars — the Sun included — got their start. Each piece pairs Chandra’s X-ray data with views from other NASA telescopes.

In a recent development, each sonification plays as a short video. A line sweeps across the image, and whatever it crosses becomes sound. Most of the regions also come in three versions — Chandra’s X-rays alone, the companion telescope’s data alone, and the full composite. Try a single layer first, then the composite, and you’ll start to hear which sounds are associated with which kind of light.

At around 400 light-years away, the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex is the closest star-forming region of the four. This crowded region is filled with a wide variety of stars. Chandra’s X-ray data identifies individual newborn stars, while JWST maps the other stars, gas, and dust around them. The X-rays ring out as bright, shimmering notes. Meanwhile, the clouds of dust and gas provide shifting ethereal chords, and individual stars land as crisp, percussive pings. Listen for the hush partway through — that’s a stretch of dark dust that hides almost all light.

In a recent development, about 1,310 light-years away and just below Orion’s Belt, the Orion Nebula is often visible to the naked eye and shows up in even the smallest telescope on a dark night. Chandra reveals more than 1,000 young stars here, each one sparkling in the sonification. Around them, the nebula’s diffuse X-ray glow holds steady as a ringing whistle. JWST’s infrared view of the dust and gas is audible as bent, warbling strings and a synthesized harp, reaching a crescendo in the nebula’s densest region before fading out.

Roughly 7,670 light-years away lies the ridge of gas and dust that became one of JWST’s most famous images when it was released in 2022. Chandra sees the scene differently, cutting through the dust to the hidden infant stars within it. Each of those stars plays as a quick stab, while the region’s faint X-ray glow draws out droning, unhurried notes — all played on an actual cello by musician Johnny Mok. JWST’s towering cliffs are a steady drone underneath, with new instruments chiming in briefly to denote a star or one of the cliffline’s jagged peaks.

According to recent reports, some 12 million light-years away in Ursa Major, M82 is the only object in the album beyond our galaxy. This starburst galaxy is building stars many times faster than the Milky Way. Its newborn giants burn out and explode quickly, venting superheated gas plumes that shine brightly in Chandra’s X-rays. Here, Chandra’s data joins Hubble’s visible-light view and infrared from JWST and the retired Spitzer Space Telescope. X-rays sit at the very top of the register, with the region’s busy center whooshing like moving air, filling most of the audible spectrum. It is punctuated by sharp, short stings from brighter newborn stars. The infrared rumbles below as a low hum interrupted by picked notes, and visible light fills the middle with a variety of sounds, including sweeping chords that rise and fall with optical brightness.

According to recent reports, the Chandra sonifications come from a team led by visualization scientist Kimberly Arcand of the Chandra X-ray Center, working with astrophysicist Matt Russo and musician Andrew Santaguida of the SYSTEM Sounds project and consultant Christine Malec, a blind astronomer and musician. You can hear all four at the Chandra release page, and find the program’s full back catalog at chandra.si.edu/sound.

Where Chandra’s fresh album is composed by others, Skysynth lets you become the composer. Built by the same SYSTEM Sounds duo of Russo and Santaguida for the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s SkyViewer app, it lets you roam Rubin’s ultra-wide view of the southern sky — press Play to coast, or steer with your arrow keys or by dragging with the mouse. Galaxies crossing the center of the screen strum a harp and stars ring a glockenspiel, with color setting the pitch and brightness the volume.

Try it at skyviewer.app/skysynth.

In a recent development, brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

#54311. What satellites leave behind

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3219 w)

What satellites leave behind

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3219 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was the lithium that gave it away, claims Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
  • It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.
  • Their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was the lithium that gave it away, claims Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.

Their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering. The team hoped to get a baseline measurement of the chemistry of the upper atmosphere, before any geoengineering experiments altered the hard-to-reach atmospheric layer.

The lithium showed they were too late.

The team expected to find trace amounts of metals naturally deposited by meteoroids, which constantly bombard and burn up in Earth’s atmosphere. But their data revealed way more lithium in stratospheric particles than is typically present in meteoroids.

“That’s what led us to the other metals,” Murphy says. Analyzing their samples, they also found higher than expected levels of aluminum, plus significant amounts of other metals like copper and lead that are scarcely found in meteoroids and must have come from some other source. Then there were the more exotic metals like niobium and hafnium, which appeared in their samples in the same ratio as in an alloy used to manufacture rocket engine nozzles.

In a recent development, the data pointed to an obvious culprit: human-made objects such as satellites and spent rocket stages that fall back to Earth from orbit and reenter the atmosphere. On the way down, they wear away and disintegrate under the heat of friction — a process known as ablation.

Later that year in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Murphy and his colleagues reported that 10% of stratospheric aerosol particles carried metals from spacecraft.

The number was shocking, but not altogether surprising. Reentries have been rising sharply in recent years as corporations and countries began launching megaconstellations of thousands of satellites, like SpaceX’s Starlink. And all those satellites will inevitably deorbit.

It has been revealed that since Murphy and his colleagues’ 2023 report, it’s become clear that human-made satellites are now dumping more of certain metals into the upper atmosphere than meteoroids naturally do. This influx has raised concerns that the metals might catalyze chemical reactions that destroy ozone, alter cloud formation, or boost or buffer the greenhouse effect.

In a recent development, researchers say it’s too soon to know for sure if the metals are a serious environmental problem. But megaconstellations are growing faster than our ability to close these knowledge gaps.

It has been revealed that at the same time, the uncertainty over whether regulators might have to act presents a big risk to the space industry, says Martin Ross of the Aerospace Corporation, a research and development nonprofit based in El Segundo, California, and a co-author of the 2023 study. “We would call it an enterprise risk,” says Ross, “in that the longer we wait to see if there is something going on, the bigger the mitigation will be — if there needs to be any mitigation — down the line.”.

From our vantage point on Earth, space may be incomprehensibly vast, but the orbital environment is not.

It has been revealed that six years ago, according to the U.S. Space Force’s public catalog, there were some 13,700 trackable objects circling in low Earth orbit; last year, the number had climbed to nearly 25,000. Disposing of satellites in the atmosphere reduces overcrowding and the risk of uncontrolled objects crashing into each other — and potentially setting off a chain of collisions that wipe out key space-based technologies or turn Earth orbit into an impenetrable debris field.

RELATED: Our increasingly cluttered skies.

Recent findings suggest that “Reentry is the only sustainable, short-term way of cleaning up the orbital environment,” says José Pedro Ferreira, a doctoral candidate in astronautical engineering at the University of Southern California (USC) in Los Angeles, who left an industry job for academia in the early 2020s when it became clear that reentry could have unintended consequences. “We need to do it, otherwise we may undermine our capability of accessing orbit.”.

But operators are also typically held responsible by their national regulators for any damages their spacecraft cause on the ground, and for decades the industry has designed spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere to minimize the risk to lives and infrastructure on the ground, a principle known as design for demise.

As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

“As with everything, we live in a closed system,” says Ferreira, “and things do not disappear.”.

SpaceX debuted its first 60 satellites into orbit in May 2019 to bring internet to even remote regions of the globe; less than a decade later, Starlink’s constellation is more than 10,000 satellites strong. Starlink already comprises roughly two-thirds of active satellites, and SpaceX plans to grow it to as many as 42,000. Other countries and corporations are not far behind: Amazon Leo is authorized by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to operate roughly 7,700 satellites; China has plans to deploy some 28,000.

Not only are we launching more than ever, but we’re also bringing spacecraft back down faster than ever before.

According to recent reports, for decades, spacecraft have been designed to burn up as much as possible upon reentry to minimize risks to those on the ground. As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

Recent findings suggest that historically, satellite operators had what Ferreira calls a “gentleman’s agreement” to deorbit their spacecraft within 25 years of mission termination to prevent orbital clutter. Recently, some national authorities have begun enforcing even tighter timelines. The FCC, for example, now enforces a five-year window.

“If you have 50,000 satellites in orbit, which is almost surely going to be reached in the not too distant future, with a design lifetime of five years,” Murphy says, “that would mean a satellite would be reentering and burning up in the atmosphere on average more than once an hour.”.

Operators of megaconstellations may use even shorter timelines for deorbiting satellites, according to Ferreira, bringing them down at the first sign of malfunction. “Which is great from a standpoint of orbital sustainability,” he says, “but it starts raising the question more and more about what the impacts are in the atmosphere.”.

There are reasons to be concerned.

Recent findings suggest that aluminum, for example, which makes up the bulk of most spacecraft, may form aluminum oxides as it breaks down during ablation, which can kick-start a chain of chemical reactions that eat away at ozone, Earth’s main shield against UV radiation. Some atmospheric models suggest that metals from spacecraft in stratospheric particles could seed polar stratospheric clouds, further accelerating ozone depletion.

Sources indicate that injecting aluminum into the upper atmosphere is also the basis of many controversial geoengineering looks. Aluminum compounds would block radiation from the Sun, which could cool down our warming planet. But they might also entrap radiation reflected off the surface of the ocean, which could increase surface temperatures. Opposition to geoengineering has so far stymied any field experiments, but with the number of reentries rising from a few hundred to many thousands per year, an uncontrolled geoengineering experiment on a grand scale may have already begun.

Recent findings suggest that “The metals are at the same altitude range as the ozone layer, so we have to be concerned about what they would do,” Murphy indicates. “We don’t know it’s bad, but we don’t know it isn’t bad either.”.

One reason it’s so difficult to predict the impacts of ablation is that we don’t yet understand what happens to spacecraft during ablation. “We reenter things all the time and we have been since the moment we started launching spacecraft,” says Stijn Lemmens, a space debris mitigation analyst at the European Space Agency (ESA). “It’s fascinating, for something which is so ubiquitous, how little we actually know about it, and how little we used to care about it.”.

Operators have long been incentivized to design spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere, and decades of this design for demise ethos has given the space industry a solid idea of how much material — or how little — will make it to the ground when objects burn through the atmosphere.

But in terms of that material that is ablated, “we’re really in the dark,” notes Ross. Previous studies have suggested that around 90% of the bodies of orbiting satellites and spent upper stages could be vaporized, later condensing into the nanosized particles the team detected. But, says Ross, “we really don’t understand how these vehicles melt, how they break apart, how they form smoke trails.”.

To quantify the impacts on the atmosphere, researchers start with atmospheric models and then add ablated material, examining how those particles interact with the natural stratospheric background via complex chemical reactions and physical processes like mixing. But the outputs of the atmospheric models are right now held back by our limited understanding of the fiery, complex process of ablation — details like what compounds are being emitted and what size particles are being formed. “We’re basically guessing at this point,” Ross states. “And we’re getting to the limit of what we can do with guessing.”.

To do better, scientists are developing newly introduced models of the physics and chemistry of ablation itself. At USC, Ferreira and his colleagues model how ablation produces aluminum oxides in the upper atmosphere, providing atmospheric researchers with inputs for both emissions and particle size. In a 2024 study in Geophysical Research Letters, the team reported that a 550-pound (250 kilograms) satellite — about the size of your average megaconstellation satellite — could deposit some 66 pounds (30 kg) of aluminum oxide nanoparticles in the upper atmosphere. Such particles could remain aloft for upwards of 30 years, potentially catalyzing ozone-destroying reactions as they settle throughout the stratosphere for decades after reentry.

Recent findings suggest that but state-of-the-art ablation models don’t always agree on what products are being formed, according to Ross. A model from researchers at the University of Leeds in the U.K. suggests that aluminum hydroxide, rather than aluminum oxide, may be the main byproduct.

To validate ablation models and get more useful data from atmospheric models, we need more measurements from reentries. How an object breaks apart as it tumbles through the air is a messy process — a product of astrophysics, fluid mechanics, materials science, and engineering. “You cannot reproduce it on Earth,” Lemmens claims. “There is no facility large enough to, in one assessment, combine all the effects.”.

That means scientists need to measure ablation where it’s actually taking place — “take instruments and put them on airplanes and go out and watch these things reenter,” Ross says.

Sources indicate that since the beginning of the Space Age, these kinds of measurements have only been taken a handful of times. Observing space objects from an airplane as they streak through the atmosphere is difficult work — and potentially dangerous. Most reentering objects are uncontrolled, making it hard to predict exactly where the object will hit the atmosphere and how much of it will burn up in the process. Researchers need a degree of certainty to avoid sending a plane full of scientists and sensors up into a debris field. “These types of reentries, which are destructive and still predictable so that you can get close, are extremely rare,” Lemmens says.

But in 2024, ESA got lucky. The first of four Cluster II satellites — rolled out in 2000 to study Earth’s magnetosphere — was poised to reenter the atmosphere, and the agency had a pretty good idea of exactly where and when it would break up over the southern Pacific Ocean.

“We could get close,” Lemmens claims. “The drawback is it was in broad daylight, which had not been attempted before on this level of detail.”.

In daytime, the team would have no visual confirmation of reentry, and it would be harder to get clean data than at night. The team had to trust they were pointing their instruments at the right spot, and then look at their data after the fact to see if they caught it. “In the end, it’s a leap of faith,” Lemmens says. “You predict as well as you can, you fly the plane as well as you can, but in the end, you do it all in the blind,” he says.

On Sept. 8, a team of scientists took off from Easter Island on a modified Dassault Falcon 900 business jet packed with instruments, and pointed their cameras just above the bright blue horizon roughly 500 miles (800 km) away.

The team used spectroscopic instruments to identify which vapors were coming from the ablating satellite. Since the team knew the material makeup of the satellite, they could gauge its surface temperatures during reentry, as the appearance of specific ions would indicate a certain material had reached its melting point.

In a recent development, altogether, they captured about 20 seconds of the reentry. Two more satellites from the same cluster were set to reenter within 24 hours of each other on Aug. 31 and Sept. 1, 2026, giving ESA another opportunity to capture more of the reentry process and to fully reconstruct the breakup.

For researchers, one upside to the rapid and unmitigated increase in satellite reentries is more opportunities to capture the process in action.

Some of the best data yet to come will be collected by ESA’s Draco mission, in which the agency aims to build and launch a satellite with the “sole purpose of falling apart again,” says Lemmens. Draco will launch in 2027 with an indestructible capsule that will survive reentry, protecting the data collected from the surface of the satellite as it’s torn apart by the atmosphere.

Researchers will be able to combine these onboard data with remote observations, using them to improve or validate existing models of ablation. “That means we, for the first time, will actually have the full story without any ambiguities,” Lemmens says.

Once a scientific consensus is reached, then mitigation measures, whether technological or regulatory, can be deployed.

Industry observers note that if research confirms that one material or another in spacecraft is particularly damaging to the atmosphere, for example, space operators can remove and replace it. “That was the basis of the success of the Montreal Protocol,” notes Ross.

After scientists discovered a hole in the ozone layer in the 1980s, every country in the world signed on to the Montreal Protocol, an international agreement to control the ozone-depleting substances humans were emitting into the atmosphere. The hole has been shrinking ever since. Signed in 1987, the agreement is widely considered one of the most successful environmental treaties to date. Since then, however, other global climate agreements have not fared as well.

Still, many remain optimistic, including Ross. He points to the commercial space industry’s track record of working with regulators and astronomers to reduce space debris and light pollution. “There is some current flowing in those lines,” he notes.

RELATED: Can robots save Earth orbit?

Recent findings suggest that some operators have already expressed a commitment to acting on whatever guidelines come out of research on the atmospheric risks. “The difficulty that I have as a responsible operator is, in this particular case, I don’t know what to do,” Vijay Thakur, a technical authority at French satellite corporation Eutelsat, said at an October 2025 panel at the Secure World Foundation’s 7th Summit for Space Sustainability in Paris. There are clear brightness limits he can follow to mitigate impacts to the astronomical community, he noted, but no such guidelines exist yet for atmospheric impacts.

“I want to put the right technical requirements, for me as the operator customer, onto industry so they can build what I need to operate and take it up and bring it back down without damaging anything from 0 kilometers to the von Kármán line,” Thakur remarked, referring to the commonly accepted boundary of outer space at 62 miles high (100 km). “Help.”.

There are some design tweaks at the moment available that could reduce emissions and help more of each spacecraft survive reentry, including non-ablative heat shields and inflatable aerodynamic decelerators, according to Adam Mitchell, a materials and processes evaluation engineer at ESA.

It has been revealed that of course, the more of a spacecraft that survives reentry, the greater the risk on the ground during uncontrolled reentries — and most reentries are uncontrolled. “There is this balance between sustainability and safety, but when it comes to human safety, there is no compromise at all,” Chris Young, space sustainability senior lead at the U.K. Space Agency, stated at the same Secure World Foundation panel. “Design for demise has to take priority.”.

Industry observers note that satellite builders could also consider replacing problematic metals — but that comes with its own trade-offs. In 2024, the world’s first wooden satellite, LignoSat, released to orbit in a partnership between Kyoto University and Japanese logging firm Sumitomo Forestry. A cube of magnolia wood panels, LignoSat will give researchers insights into how well wood holds up in the space environment, and how cleanly it burns up in the atmosphere. Carbon fiber is another material of interest, according to Ferreira. But these organic materials may release black carbon into the upper atmosphere, which may absorb sunlight or reflect it, depending on the structure the carbon takes.

Ross thinks we can close the remaining knowledge gaps in short order — and that those lessons can be applied almost immediately. “We can do that before the next generation of satellites comes along,” he states, “but we just need the resources.”.

A cultural revolution is coming for the industry, regardless of what’s discovered about the impacts to the atmosphere. “The one-use, nonrecyclable culture that we have in space, of, ‘We’ll launch something to space with rare Earth minerals that are of limited supply and then burn them all up in the atmosphere after one use,’ that is unsustainable,” said Young.

A sustainable future — one that balances both Earth and space sustainability — will involve creating something we haven’t quite nailed yet in our earthbound industries. “We need to move beyond the single-use mindset that right now defines much of spacecraft design and accelerate the transition toward an in-space circular economy,” Mitchell indicates.

Can we do in space what we’ve failed to do on Earth? Right now, researchers are gathering data as fast as they can, as fast as resourcing allows, to inform models of ablation and atmospheric processes that will eventually be validated by measurements taken during reentry.

Then, equipped with actionable data, we can act.

Kate Wheeling is a freelance journalist based in Santa Barbara, California. She writes about the environment and humans’ relationship with the natural world. Her work has appeared in The Atlantic, Smithsonian magazine, The Daily Beast, and Mother Jones.

The Sky This Week from November 20 to 27: Uranus at opposition

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M.
  • In the northeast, Auriga the Charioteer is above the horizon by 7 P.M.
  • Capella’s name essentially means “She-Goat,” according to the late stellar expert Jim Kaler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST, then passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. They remain visible all evening, forming a triangle in southern Pisces and northern Cetus. The Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, but Neptune will be invisible without binoculars or a telescope. Check out last week’s column for more details on how to view the celestial trio.

In the northeast, Auriga the Charioteer is above the horizon by 7 P.M. local time. Its brightest star is Capella, which shines at magnitude 0.1 and sits some 43 light-years away. Just southeast of this star, you’ll find another triangle in the sky tonight. This small shape is an asterism about 2.7° long, known as the Kids. It consists of Epsilon (ε), Zeta (ζ), and Eta (η) Aurigae, which range from 3rd (Epsilon and Eta) to 4th (Zeta) magnitude.

Why are these called the Kids? Capella’s name essentially means “She-Goat,” according to the late stellar expert Jim Kaler. These fainter stars cluster close by the brighter star like goat kids around their mother.

Mercury reaches greatest western elongation (20°) at 7 P.M. EST; it will be visible before dawn tomorrow morning, so keep reading for more details.

It has been revealed that sunrise: 6:51 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 2:04 P.M. Moonset: 2:12 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Saturday, November 21If you’ve got a viewing site with a clear eastern horizon, this morning offers a great opportunity to spot the solar system’s innermost planet. Look for Mercury about an hour before sunrise, when it reaches 7° high and shines at magnitude –0.5. The planet reached its greatest western elongation from our Sun yesterday evening, and is now 20° west of our star in the sky.

Recent findings suggest that located in Libra, the tiny world sits to the far lower left of bright Venus, higher in the sky. Venus is in the constellation Virgo, standing just north (to the upper left) of the bright star Spica. Another bright star, Arcturus in Boötes, hangs to that pair’s far upper left.

Sources indicate that pull out a telescope to check out the size and phase of each planet. Start with Venus, whose disk spans a hefty 46” — right now larger than Jupiter’s apparent size in our sky. Despite its impressive width, however, the disk of Venus appears as just a sliver, only 19% lit. Slide down to Mercury for comparison, and see that its phase is much larger — 62% — while the planet’s overall apparent width is much smaller, just 7”.

In a recent development, if you’re able, keep watching Mercury day by day in the morning sky. Its gibbous phase will continue growing, reaching 84% lit by the end of the month.

Sunrise: 6:52 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:29 P.M. Moonset: 3:22 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (92%).

Sunday, November 22With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape. The large, flat-floored crater Schickard is prominent in the southwest, near the small, circular Mare Humorum. Because the nearly Full Moon is so bright, you may want to use a Moon filter before you turn your telescope toward our satellite tonight for a closer look.

In a recent development, zoom in on Schickard to discover that its dark floor isn’t perfectly smooth, but pockmarked by smaller craters that came after the initial, larger crater’s formation. Its outer walls are shallow and beaten down, also showing off their age. Look closely at Schickard’s western wall to see how it has slumped, particularly compared to the eastern side of the crater rim. Also compare the texture of the southwestern portion of the crater floor, which appears quite rough, to the rest of the crater, which is smoother. The difference arises because most of the crater was flooded by lava, which didn’t quite reach its southwestern regions.

Recent findings suggest that stretching about 130 miles (210 kilometers) across, Schickard is roughly 4 billion years old and was formed by a giant impact. Because it sits so near the limb of the Moon, it often looks oblong from our vantage point on Earth — but from above, orbiters have shown it is really quite circular in shape.

Sunrise: 6:53 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:59 P.M. Moonset: 4:34 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (97%).

Monday, November 23A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Industry observers note that glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

Recent findings suggest that if you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

Sunrise: 6:54 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 3:37 P.M. Moonset: 5:52 A.M. Moon Phase: Full.

It has been revealed that tuesday, November 24Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon.

In a recent development, A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so significant and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed promptly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

It has been revealed that the Moon then passes 5° north of Uranus (also in Taurus) at 2 P.M. EST. Over in the constellation Leo, Mars passes 1.8° north of Regulus at 5 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 6:55 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 4:24 P.M. Moonset: 7:10 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (99%).

Recent findings suggest that wednesday, November 25The Moon reaches perigee, the closest point to Earth in its orbit, at 4:01 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will stand 223,288 miles (359,347 km) away.

Recent findings suggest that the distant ice giant Uranus reaches opposition tonight at 6 P.M. EST. Opposition is the best time to view a planet in our sky, and it’s visible roughly from dusk until dawn. Because Uranus is faint — magnitude 5.6 — you’ll want to give it a few hours after sunset to climb away from both light pollution and turbulent air near the horizon. Around 10 P.M. local time, you’ll find Uranus midway between the bright star Aldebaran and the Pleiades star cluster in Taurus the Bull, about 60° above the southeastern horizon. It sits some 1.5° south of 4th-magnitude 37 Tauri.

Sources indicate that although Uranus can be visible to the naked eye under clear, dark conditions, the bright waning Moon is nearby, so pull out binoculars or a telescope to view the far-off planet tonight. Once you land on its location, look for a “flat,” grayish-colored star. Uranus’ disk spans 4”, so you will likely be able to tell it is circular, rather than a pinpoint of light like any background stars.

Industry observers note that sunrise: 6:56 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 5:24 P.M. Moonset: 8:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (96%).

Thursday, November 26Celebrate Thanksgiving with a celestial turkey: The famous Orion Nebula (M42) is also playfully known as the Turkey Nebula because it looks to some like a turkey, particularly in deep astrophotos. But whether you’re a photographer or not, this bright deep-sky treat is easy to enjoy tonight while dinner digests.

It has been revealed that by about 9 P.M. local time, Orion the Hunter has risen above the eastern horizon, his recognizable three-star belt standing in a vertical line. The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. You might be able to spot its glow without optical aid, although the bright Moon nearby may make that difficult. Binoculars or any telescope will easily show it.

It has been revealed that at 4th magnitude and spanning some 85’ by 60’, the Orion Nebula is a huge and bright star-forming region that sits roughly 1,350 light-years from Earth. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.

Sunrise: 6:58 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 6:35 P.M. Moonset: 9:33 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (91%).

Sources indicate that friday, November 27The Moon-free window for observing Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS reopens tonight, the same day the comet reaches perihelion, the closest point to the Sun in its 21½-year orbit. It has been a fairly stable 10th to 11th magnitude, and although it has no appreciable tail, the nucleus’ green glow has been notable in recent astrophotos.

It has been revealed that you’ll find Hartley-IRAS in the west a few hours after sunset. Around 7 P.M. local time it is still 30° high, well above the turbulent air near the ground that can muddy astronomical views. Tonight the comet is in western Sagitta, about 6.3° north-northeast of 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Aquilae. Even a small (4-inch) scope will net you a view, but larger apertures will show more detail around the nucleus, allowing you to look for features such as a sharpened southern flank as it flies into the solar headwind.

While you’re in this region, make sure to sweep just 2.1° northeast of the comet’s location to spot the famous Coathanger asterism in Vulpecula. This 1°-long grouping of stars looks just like its namesake, with the hook on the southern side of the hanger’s arms.

Sunrise: 6:59 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 7:53 P.M. Moonset: 10:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%).

A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations.
  • “They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” indicates the narrator of the 1966 movie version.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In the classic Dr. Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations. Poised to throw it all off a mountain, the grumpy loner has a change of heart as joyous song rises from Whoville.

“They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” indicates the narrator of the 1966 movie version. With a beatific smile, he pulls the stolen goods back from the brink and returns everything.

According to recent reports, would a too-small heart make you grumpy like the Grinch? And what would happen if your heart went from too small to really massive in an instant? The answer depends on what causes the heart to shrink or swell, experts say. And whether or not you are a snake.

Heart size is generally pegged to body size, indicates Michelle Kittleson, a cardiologist at Cedars Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles. Bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. But some people, she says, have hearts that are naturally bigger or smaller than average for their bodies. It’s not clear why. However, she says, “there are negative consequences of having a too-small heart.”.

In one 2025 study, researchers looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people in Australia. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts, the team reported in JACC: Advances.

It has been revealed that smaller hearts may not pump blood as well as larger ones, making it harder for people to exercise. And if the Grinch didn’t exercise enough, maybe “then that made him really tired, and that made him grumpy,” Kittleson states. “Or maybe he did the research, and he found out that his life expectancy was shortened because of it, and that made him even grumpier.”.

But would rapidly increasing his heart’s size be good for the Grinch?

As the Grinch slides downhill toward Whoville, pulled by a sled piled high with presents he’d stolen and now was returning, he physically undergoes a change. What started as a heart two sizes too small swelled three sizes, both curing his grumpiness and giving him super strength. Or so the classic tale goes. A person going through such a dramatic change may not fare as well.

Recent findings suggest that there are many ways a heart can grow, says Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder. With vigorous exercise, “your heart gets bigger in good ways,” Leinwand says. That can be true for athletes who do lots of cardio, such as swimmers and marathon runners.

“Their heart gets bigger and thicker,” Kittleson says. “But it’s a good thing in them because it helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.” Pregnancy also makes the whole organ expand to boost blood to the developing fetus. If people stop exercising, or give birth, their hearts will shrink back to normal size within months.

Some diseases, though, can enlarge hearts in deadly ways. “If you’ve got untreated high blood pressure,” Leinwand indicates, “you can get a huge heart, and it’s not good for you.”.

It has been revealed that stress, bad heart valves and some genetic diseases can also result in bigger, but weaker, hearts. In those cases, the heart muscle grows in order to pump more blood. At the same time, the inside of the left ventricle — the heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the body — can shrink. That makes it harder for the heart to push blood out. This kind of growth takes time, Kittleson says.

Recent findings suggest that there is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly. Called takotsubo or stress cardiomyopathy — or in some cases, broken-heart syndrome — it is brought on by extreme stress. That can include positive things like winning the lottery or entering a surprise party or negative stress such as break-up or losing a job.

According to recent reports, A surge of epinephrine, or adrenaline, from stress can make the left ventricle bulge into the shape of a pot used to catch octopuses. (Takotsubo is Japanese for “octopus pot.”) That causes immediate heart failure as the heart chamber gets too big to pump blood.

It has been revealed that so instead of becoming super strong, the Grinch “would have keeled over and collapsed,” Kittleson says. (People can survive with prompt medical care and their hearts can return to normal size in a few months.).

Given the Grinch survived his rapid growth, there’s another possible scenario: Maybe his heart is more like a snake’s.

Sources indicate that pythons’ hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day after the snakes eat a large meal — sometimes as big as an adult deer. And the bigger a python’s meal, the more its heart grows. Larger hearts pump blood with more force, Leinwand and her colleagues reported in 2024 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers don’t know if this makes the snakes stronger overall.

Sources indicate that once a meal is digested, the heart shrinks again. Snakes can go through many shrink-and-grow cycles with no ill effect. Leinwand hopes that studying these snakes will lead to treatments that make human hearts healthier.

Recent findings suggest that but becoming kinder, like the Grinch? Maybe not.

Notes Leinwand, “our snakes, when they eat a lot, they get rather aggressive.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 19: Mercury moves into Libra.

The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

From the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan. Saturn is the brightest object in this part of the sky after the Moon, so you don’t have to worry about misidentifying it. After passing south of the ringed world earlier this week, Titan now sits about 3.2’ to Saturn’s west, in line with the rings. Fainter moons Tethys, Rhea, and Dione may be visible clustered closer to the planet, but the bright moonlight might also make them challenging for visual observation.

From Saturn, scan 6.6° west-southwest to land on Neptune. If you have a go-to scope, it may take you right to the outermost planet, which glows at magnitude 7.7 and offers up a tiny, 2”-wide disk. It may look like a “flat,” bluish-gray star, rather than a bright pinprick of white light. Look for a large parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars just over 9° to Saturn’s southwest if you need a closer stepping stone. The star at the northeastern point of that shape is 5th-magnitude 29 Piscium, and it lies about 2.6° southwest of Neptune.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, former Rep.
  • Recent findings suggest that former Rep.
  • In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call).

Recent findings suggest that former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family confirmed.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

“Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”.

When McDermott confirmed his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”.

Born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

He attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against newly introduced sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a newly introduced life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

Recent findings suggest that “I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”.

In a recent development, as he said, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

Industry observers note that then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

Industry observers note that mcDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

“Jim McDermott was as massive as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”.

Dan Bartlett from June Lake, California.

Recent findings suggest that asteroid 6993 (1995 BJ4), a small body 7 miles (11 kilometers) across, orbits in the main belt between Mars and Jupiter. In August 2026, astronomers spotted a faint tail, making it candidate for the largest known main-belt comet. However, the tail has been gradually fading through 2026, which hints at it being caused by debris from a one-time impact rather than ongoing outgassing, astronomers reported last month in a paper accepted in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. In this image, the tail spans more than 35′, or wider than the Full Moon.

4.6 hours of exposure with two 11-inch f/2.2 Celestron RASA telescopes, ZWO ASI6200MM Pro (monochrome) and ZWO ASI6200MC Pro (one-shot color) cameras.

2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon.
  • The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m.
  • We’ll patch this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll patch this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.).

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

Sources indicate that the times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column.

In a recent development, friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M.Sunset: 4:40 P.M.Moonrise: 2:04 P.M.Moonset: 2:12 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%).

Sunrise: 6:52 A.M.Sunset: 4:39 P.M.Moonrise: 2:29 P.M.Moonset: 3:22 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (92%).

Industry observers note that sunday, November 22With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape. The large, flat-floored crater Schickard is prominent in the southwest, near the small, circular Mare Humorum.

Stretching about 130 miles (210 kilometers) across, Schickard is roughly 4 billion years old and was formed by a giant impact. Because it sits so near the limb of the Moon, it often looks oblong from our vantage point on Earth — but from above, orbiters have shown it is really quite circular in shape.

Sunrise: 6:53 A.M.Sunset: 4:39 P.M.Moonrise: 2:59 P.M.Moonset: 4:34 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (97%).

In a recent development, tuesday, November 24Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon.

A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope. The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

Sources indicate that the 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

In a recent development, the Moon then passes 5° north of Uranus, also in Taurus, at 2 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 6:55 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 4:24 P.M.Moonset: 7:10 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (99%).

Recent findings suggest that wednesday, November 25The Moon reaches perigee, the closest point to Earth in its orbit, at 4:01 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will stand 223,288 miles (359,347 km) away.

Sunrise: 6:56 A.M.Sunset: 4:37 P.M.Moonrise: 5:24 P.M.Moonset: 8:26 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (96%).

Thursday, November 26Sunrise: 6:58 A.M.Sunset: 4:37 P.M.Moonrise: 6:35 P.M.Moonset: 9:33 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (91%).

Friday, November 27Sunrise: 6:59 A.M.Sunset: 4:36 P.M.Moonrise: 7:53 P.M.Moonset: 10:26 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%).

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

RELATED: 20 things to see on the Moon.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

It has been revealed that super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Recent findings suggest that blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four Upcoming Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

It has been revealed that harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

According to recent reports, what is the difference between a Full Moon and a Upcoming Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

According to recent reports, how does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and Newly introduced Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Anna Mattson and Science News Staff.

Industry observers note that science News staff devoured books of all kinds this year, on topics ranging from ecology and evolution to the human brain and mathematics. We covered it all — even a cookbook! These 10 titles rose to the top of our 2026 reading list and could make great gifts for the book lovers in your life. —  Anna Mattson, Assistant Editor.

Massive thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers. “When I think of big numbers, I usually think of a 1 with a lot of zeroes tacked on the end. But the reality is much more complex than I ever imagined,” claims senior physics writer Emily Conover. The book, among Conover’s favorites of the year, “provided me with a fresh appreciation of our number system and the creative ways mathematicians have expanded it to express ever-larger numbers,” she says. “Plus, contemplating unfathomably large figures makes my own concerns seem insignificant.”.

According to recent reports, staff writer Erin Garcia de Jesús’ favorite book of 2026, The Creatures’ Guide to Caring, will strike a chord with newly introduced parents. “Between sleepless nights and poopy diapers, there’s not much to laugh about in the early days of parenting. But I found plenty of humor (and plenty to be grossed out about) in The Creatures’ Guide to Caring,” Garcia de Jesús indicates. “It’s the perfect book to make anyone, parent or otherwise, feel better that we’re not the only animals struggling with our offspring.”.

According to recent reports, merritt R. TuretskyW.W. Norton & Firm | $29.99.

Industry observers note that adventure seekers will lose themselves in the mesmerizing ecosystems at the heart of Bogland, biomedical sciences writer Aimee Cunningham’s favorite book of the year. Ecologist Merritt R. Turetsky immerses readers in these waterlogged landscapes that are often overlooked and underestimated. “I am firmly on team boglands after reading about the beauty and wonder of these ecosystems,” Cunningham says.

Saul Justin NewmanThe MIT Press | $29.95.

It has been revealed that senior writer Meghan Rosen’s favorite book of 2026 is perfect for anyone interested in — or wary of — health and wellness culture. Morbid exposes the lack of science behind a lot of antiaging advice, such as eating like centenarians do and taking “anti­aging” supplements. “Turns out, a lot of it is just plain bunk,” Rosen says. “Skeptical readers will enjoy Newman’s takedowns, which go down smoothly with a healthy dose of humor.”.

Susana CarmonaThe MIT Press | $27.95.

Senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders’ pick for 2026 is a must-read for any expecting mother, new mother or person looking to learn about how pregnancy and motherhood impact the body. “A Mother’s Brain reads like a scientific love letter to moms, who all too often get overlooked,” she notes. Author and neuroscientist Susana Carmona “covers the nascent field of matrescence in lively, vivid chapters. And along the way, she convincingly argues that the maternal brain is compelling, wondrous and still mysterious,” Sanders says.

Aaron MahnkeRunning Press | $30.00.

Those who listen to true crime podcasts or wish spooky season lasted all year long will enjoy Exhumed, an exploration of the lore and medical practices leading up to the 19th century New England vampire panic. “Thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down,” assistant editor Anna Mattson wrote in her online review. Mattson notes that Exhumed, her favorite read of 2026, is littered with bizarre facts that would be perfect for invigorating dull conversations.

For the anthropologist in your life, try The Story of Stories — a deep dive into how technological upheavals have shaped storytelling throughout history. The author provides what Sanders describes as scattershot history lessons in her online review: “Ashton has a knack for pulling out memorable bits from historical records, scientific studies and other sources for readers.”.

Alexis Nikole NelsonSimon & Schuster | $35.00.

Conover couldn’t pick just one favorite. For people who enjoy getting creative in the kitchen, she recommends Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! “This cookbook provides such a joyful how-to on foraging and eating wild plants,” Conover states. “It helped me see my plant neighbors in a whole latest light. And I got to make some tasty treats to share with my family as well.”.

It has been revealed that riley BlackSt. Martin’s Press | $29.00.

Tyrant Lizard Queen is the only work of fiction on our list. But it’s rooted in real science, and stars a Tyrannosaurus rex. Author Riley Black “offers an empathetic look at a real-life creature that experienced hunger and pain, much like the animals that surround us today,” says Science News Explores assistant editor Aaron Tremper, who chose the book as his favorite of 2026. “Black’s penchant for story makes for a thrilling read that fans of Jurassic Park and King Kong can get behind.”.

Industry observers note that joshua D. MezrichThe MIT Press | $29.95.

Sources indicate that and for those interested in bioethics, we suggest picking up Every Living Creature. Author and physician Joshua D. Mezrich offers a comprehensive look at the field of xenotransplantation, through the stories of courageous doctors and patients who helped make it possible. “At times, the story can feel like a whirlwind, whisking readers across decades and from lab to lab and surgery to surgery,” Rosen wrote in her online review. “But at its core, Every Living Creature is a book about hope.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After more than 20 years of planning, construction, and testing, astronomers have officially started the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST).
  • Richard Talcott is a former senior editor and current contributing editor of Astronomy.

After more than 20 years of planning, construction, and testing, astronomers have officially started the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). The survey will snap about 1,000 images per night with a 3.2-gigapixel camera — the largest digital camera in the world — attached to the 8.4-meter telescope at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile. The LSST will observe the entire southern sky every three to four nights, on average, across its 10-year lifetime. The goal: build a high-definition, time-lapse record of the cosmos from the solar system to distant galaxies. This part of the initial image covers about 1.7° by 1.7° centered in northeastern Centaurus, though the left side bleeds into Lupus. The wispy swirls are tenuous clouds of gas and dust known as galactic cirrus, illuminated by the diffuse glow of the Milky Way.

Richard Talcott is a former senior editor and current contributing editor of Astronomy.

The 8 Best Hot Tubs That You Can Buy Online
